p.note: : Titus bore the cognomen of his father Vespasian; his brother took the cognomen “Domitianus" from their mother Domitilla (Vesp. 3). Titus' full name was Titus Flavius Vespasianus, the nomen gentilicium “Flavius" being found only in C.I.L. xiv 3902. In early inscriptions under Vespasian he appears as Vespasianus Caesar (C.I.L. iii p. 849, x 8110, vi 346, etc.; Newton 30, 299, 324, 325); in authors he is called simply Titus (Tacitus once calls him Titus Vespasianus, H. ii 1); so in C.I.L. x 5405, Newton 168, and frequently on coins (Eckhel, vi 350-364; Cohen, i² 428-464). vir

: cf. Eutrop. vii 21, Titus omnium virtutum genere mirabilis, adeo ut amor et deliciae humani generis diceretur: Suidas, Τίτος, βασιλεὺς ῾Ῥωμαίων, Οὐεσπασιανοῦ υἱός, ἀνὴρ πᾶν ἀρετῆς συνειληφὼς γένος, ὡς πρὸς ἁπάντων ἔρως τε καὶ τρυφή (deliciae) τοῦ θνητοῦ προσαγορευθῆναι γένους: Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 6, Huius sane mors adeo provinciis luctui fuit, uti, generis humani delicias appellantes, orbatum orbem deflerent. Pliny (N.H. praef. 1) addresses Titus, to whom his work is dedicated, as iucundissime; Augustine (Civ. Dei v 21) calls him suavissimus. Pacatus (Panegyr. in Theod. 11), referring to Titus, repeats the phrase amor generis humani. Ausonius (Caes. xi) characterizes him as “Felix imperio, felix brevitate regendi, | expers civilis sanguinis, orbis amor." •

: cf. Calig. 3, 1, promerendi amoris studium: Cic. Mur. 70, homines tenues unum habent in nostrum ordinem aut promerendi aut proferendi beneficii locum. Suetonius also uses promereri c. acc. pers., Aug. 3, 2, in promerendis sociis; Cic. uses de of persons, Off. ii 53, paratiores erunt ad bene de multis promerendum.
: the artfulness of Titus in courting popularity is illustrated by Suetonius in c. 8, 2.

: Dio (lxvi 18) says that men contrasted Augustus, who would not have been so loved had he not lived so long, with Titus, who would not have been so loved had he lived longer. Dio adds that if Titus had lived long, it might have been shown that he owed his fame more to good fortune than to merit: ὁ Τίτος ἐπιεικῶς ἄρξας, ἐν ἀκμῇ τῆς δόξης ἀπέθανε, τάχα ἂν ἐλεγχθείς, εἴγε ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἐβεβιώκει, ὅτι εὐτυχίᾳ πλείονι ἢ ἀρετῇ ἐχρήσατο.

: = abunde fuit, redundavit (not adfuit, as Sabellicus and others explain it). Gellius (i 22) condemns the use of superesse for adesse reo, defendere causam (a use which occurs in Suet. Aug. 56, 3), and says: Qui integre locuti sunt, magnam partem ‘‘superesse” ita dixerunt ut eo verbo significarent superfluere et supervacare atque esse supra necessarium modum.
: = et quidem; cf. Tib. 34, 2, consuerat quadriplam strenam et de manu reddere; Ner. 12, 1, etc.

: Pitiscus aptly quotes Capitol. Anton. Philos. 15, nemo fit principum quem non gravis fama perstringat, usque adeo ut etiam Marcus in sermonem venerit, etc. Titus differed from other Roman emperors, to many of whom might be applied the words of Tacitus on the kings of the Suevi, A. xii 30, subiectis, dum adipiscerentur dominationes, multa caritate, et maiore odio, postquam adepti sunt.

: for the causal sense of quando see on Vesp. 16, 3. Trachmann (op. cit. p. 37) comments on its use here: “Quando” hic non causam affert enuntiati principalis, cur Tito tantum vel ingenii vel artis vel fortunae superfuerit, sed tanquam additamentum explicativum continet, cur scriptor adiunxerit “et quod difficillimum est, in imperio"; hic enim, nisi fallor, sententiarum nexus est: tantum illi.. superfuit, et, quod difficillimum est, in imperio, id quod eo magis commemorandum vel mirandum est, quando privatus non caruit.

: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 3, ubi patriae curam suscepit, incredibile est, quantum, quem imitabatur, anteierit, praecipue clementia, liberalitate, honorificentia, ac pecuniae contemptu, quae eo amplius grata fuere, quod ex nonnullis a privato adhuc patratis, asperior luxuriaeque et avaritiae amans credebatur fore. What Suetonius says here of Titus is said of Vespasian by Ausonius (Caes. x): olim qui dubiam privato in tempore famam, | rarum aliis, princeps transtulit in melius.
: he incurred this odium through his high-handed conduct as prefect of the praetorian guard; see с. 6.
: on account of his alleged vices people predicted that he would be a second Nero; see c. 7.

: the emperor Gaius Caligula was assassinated on Jan. 24, 41 A.D.; see on Oth. 6. 1. Suetonius is wrong in his dates. Titus was born in 39, not in 41, as Suet. himself admits when he says that Titus died (81 A.D.) in his 42nd year; see on c. 11. Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2697) suggests a possible confusion with Britannicus (see c. 2) who was born in 41. Dio (lxvi 18) says correctly that Titus was 39 years, 5 months, and 25 days old when he succeeded Vespasian on June 24, 79 A.D.

: from this passage it is clear that there was an older Septizonium before the "Septizonium Severi" built in 203 A.D. by the emperor Septimius Severus at the S.E. of the Palatine to provide a stately front to his palace where it faced the Via Appia; cf. Spart. Sept. Sev. 19, 24 (where there is a variant Septizodium): Amm. Marc. xv 7, 3 (355 A.D.), cum plebs ad Septemzonium (al. -zodium) convenisset, celebrem locum, ubi operis ambitiosi nymphaeum Marcus (Aurelius) condidit. This building of Severus apparently consisted of three stories of balconies or terraces supported by columns and was destroyed in the 16th cent. by Sixtus V who used the stone for building the Vatican (Burn, Rome and the Campagna, p. 180). A "septizonium" at Lambaesus in Numidia is mentioned in C.I.L. viii 2657 (c. 225 A.D.) and a "septizodium" at some town in the Roman province of Africa, C.I.L. viii (suppl.) 14372. Various views have been held on the original meaning of “septizonium." Some suggest 2H2 that it was a structure consisting of 7 colonnades rising in tiers, each narrower than the one supporting it, and semicircular in form: others think that it rose in steps, or that it had 7 circular walls of different heights and colours like Ecbatana in Media as described in Hdt. i 98. According to Dombart (Pauly-Wissowa, ii A. 1578 sqq.), "septizonium” corresponded to ἡ ἑπτάζωνοs, which was used primarily in a spatial sense of the 7 zones into which the heavens and also the earth were divided, and then in a temporal sense of the order of rotation of the 7 planets which marked the 7 days of the week; “Septizonium,” as the name of a building, denoted an ornamental structure serving in the main as a great public calendar, displaying on its front (1) figures of the 7 planets (Saturnus, Sol, Luna, Mars, Mercurius, Juppiter, Venus), (2) the 12 signs of the zodiac marking the months, (3) the numbers of the days in the month. There were holes to receive a peg (moved daily) opposite the various planets, signs of the zodiac, and numbers of the days, so that the day of the week, the day of the month, and the month of the year were visible at a glance; see the illustrations given by Dombart in the article cited. He regards "septizodium" as a corruption of "septizonium," while Jordan-Huelsen (Topogr. Rom i 3, 100) favour the view of Maass (Die Tagesgötter 106 sqq.) that “Septizodium" meaning "The House of the Seven Planets (ἑπτὰ ζῴδια)" is the correct form, and that "Septizonium" was a vulgar distortion of this.
: see on “perinfamis,” Vitell. 2, 4.
: see on Vesp. 12.

: at the court of Claudius. The emperors granted this honour to children of illustrious families and of foreign rulers; see Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 85. His father Vespasian had risen to the highest offices at Rome under Claudius through his military achievements and the favour of Narcissus (Vesp. 4, 1). Otho's grandfather was reared in the house of Livia Augusta (Oth. 1, 1); Marcus Aurelius grew up at Hadrian's court (Capitol. Anton. Philos. 4); Agrippa, great-grandson of Herod the Great, was among those educated at the court of Claudius (Joseph. Ant. xix 360).

: born in 41 A.D., son of the emperor Claudius and Valeria Messalina. He was called at first Tiberius Claudius Germanicus, but after his father's victories in Britain (43 A.D.) the senate decreed to the son the title "Britannicus," to be his distinctive name (Claud. 27, Dio lx 22). At the instigation of his second wife Agrippina (Galb. 5, 1) Claudius adopted Domitius, her son by a former husband, into the Claudian house with the name of Nero, and gave him precedence over Britannicus. Every humiliation was inflicted on Britannicus, and when he was charged by Agrippina with disrespect towards the adopted Nero, Claudius put to death or exiled all his best instructors (Tac. 4. xii 41, optimum quemque educatorem filii exilio aut morte adficit), and he was placed under the control of persons appointed by his stepmother. Nero succeeded Claudius, and in the second year of his reign (55 A.D.) poisoned Britannicus (Suet. Ner. 33, Tac. A. xiii 16).
: see on Galb. 5, 1.

: including Sosibius, who is mentioned in Tac. A. xi 1 as “Britannici educator." Sosibius, who, as Furneaux says, was probably a freedman like Anicetus the tutor of Nero, was used as a tool by Messalina and rewarded with 1,000,000 sesterces, nominally “quod Britannicum praeceptis, Claudium consiliis iuvaret” (4. xi 4); as an instructor of Britannicus he was put to death by Claudius at the instance of Agrippina (Dio lx 32).

: the custom of forecasting a person's future from an examination of his brow by a μετωποσκόπος is referred to by Pliny (N.H. xxxv 88) when describing the marvellous fidelity of the portraits painted by Apelles: Imagines adeo similitudinis indiscretae pinxit ut—incredibile dictu Apio grammaticus scriptum reliquerit quendam ex facie hominum divinantem, quos metoposcopos vocant, ex iis dixisse aut futurae mortis annos aut praeteritae. Juvenal also mentions it, vi 583, frontemque manumque | praebebit vati crebrum poppysma roganti. Metoposcopy and Chiromancy were reckoned by Artemidorus (Oneirocr. ii 69) among the more vulgar forms of soothsaying (Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 213). physiognomon, or physiognomist, differed from the metoposcopus by telling characters, not fortunes; cf. Cic. Fat. 5, Quid? Socratem nonne legimus, quemadmodum notarit Zopyrus physiognomon, qui se profitebatur hominum mores naturasque ex corpore, oculis, vultu, fronte pernoscere? Stupidum esse Socratem dixit et bardum, addidit etiam, mulierosum: Cic. Tusc. iv 37.
: see on Vesp. 4, 1. The

: here utique means "certainly," as in Ner. 22, 1; in Tib. 47, Calig. 53, 1, and Ner. 28, 2 it means "especially"; it is used with a neg. in Ner. 15, 2, triumphalia ornamenta tribuit, nec utique (“necessarily'") de causa militari. In Cicero this adv. occurs almost exclusively in the Letters; Livy and Seneca use it very frequently.

: Suetonius (Ner. 33) describes how the first weak poison compounded by the archpoisoner (venenariorum index) Locusta proved ineffective when administered to Britannicus. Nero compelled her to make a stronger potion which was tried first on a kid, and the animal lingered for five hours. A still stronger brew was tried on a pig, which died at once, and Nero ordered this mixture to be taken to the triclinium and given to Britannicus, who dropped dead at the first taste (ad primum gustum concidit). That account hardly tallies with what Suetonius says here about Britannicus draining the draught (potione hausta), and about Titus, who tasted it, escaping death. Tacitus (A. xiii 16), describing the second attempt to poison Britannicus, says that a harmless draught of very hot wine and water was offered to him after it had been tasted in his presence, and when he rejected it as too hot, some cold water containing the virulent poison was poured in, and this proved fatal instantaneously.

: used inaccurately instead of sedens. Children sat at table and did not recline. The grandsons of Augustus sat beside him on the lowest couch; Aug. 64, 3, neque cenavit una, nisi ut in imo lecto assiderent. Claudius always had his children present at dinner along with the sons and daughters of distinguished men, and they sat at the ends (arms) of the couches as they ate: Claud. 32, adhibebat omni cenae et liberos suos cum pueris puellisque nobilibus, qui more veteri ad fulcra sedentes vescerentur. Nero kept up this custom, but the children (including Britannicus) sat at a table of their own more frugally furnished: Tac. A. xiii 16, mos habebatur principum liberos cum ceteris idem aetatis sedentes vesci in aspectu propinquorum propria et parciore mensa. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 p. 300. iactantur gravique morbo adfiictatus diu: cf. Cic. Cat. i 13, homines aegri febri deinde multo gravius adflictantur. Oudendorp's suggestion that sit has fallen out has nothing to recommend it. Suetonius expresses himself with his usual brevity, but the meaning seems clearly to be that Titus was believed to have tasted the poison and in consequence to have been prostrated by a long illness. The illness was not a matter of opinion or belief, the cause of the illness was. Fuisse is to be supplied with adflictatus; cf. Calig. 50, creditur potionatus a Caesonia: Vesp. 16, 2, creditur solitus promovere. Alexander (op. cit. p. 18) argues that -que should be regarded as an interpolation. Similarly -que is rejected by Polak in Claud. 1, 4, Fuisse autem creditur non minus gloriosi quam civilis animi; nam ex hoste super victorias opima quoque spolia captasse summoque saepius discrimine duces Germanorum tota acie insectatus. In his note on that passage Smilda defends -que as having an explicative force.
: = postea; see on Oth. 10, 1.
: cf. Oth. 1, 3.

: so among the honours decreed to Germanicus after death was "ut ludos circenses eburna effigies praeiret' (Tac. A. ii 83). In the procession at the opening of these games images of the gods were carried in litters (fercula) on the shoulders of men or in sacred cars (tensae, Vesp. 5, 7; cf. Dion. Hal. vii 72). An ivory image of Julius Caesar was borne in a tensa while he was still alive (Iul. 76, Aug. 43), and the honour was frequently decreed to the emperors after death. The pompa circensis was marshalled on the Capitoline hill, and then passed down the Sacra Via to the Forum, turned to the right through the Vicus Tuscus, the Velabrum, the Forum Boarium, and through the main entrance of the Circus (the Porta Pompae), and then passed once round the metae. For a detailed account of this brilliant spectacle see Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 44 and Mayor on Juv. x 36-46.

: = hodie quoque; see on Galb. 1. prosecutus est: in the pompa circensis. Suet. uses prosequi very frequently both in the sense of accompanying as a mark of respect (προπέμπειν), and in the general sense of honouring; e.g. Oth. 1, 3, Senatus honore rarissimo, statua in Palatio posita, prosecutus est eum: Dom. 9, 2, omnes circa se largissime prosecutus.

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 2, a puero praeclaris studiis, probitatis, militiae, litterarum, instantissime deditus, quo contenderit, animi et corporis muneribus ostendit. dos, in the sense of a bodily or mental gift or endowment, is a favourite word with Ovid, who has dos corporis, formae, oris, ingenii, etc. So in prose writers of the Silver age, e.g. Sen. Vit. Beat. 8, 2, corporis dotes. Suet. uses virtutes in the same way, e.g. Calig. 3, 1, corporis animique virtutes.

: explendescere is found earlier in Nepos, Att. 1, in pueritia nobilis inter aequales ferebatur, clariusque explendescebat. Cicero uses the simple verb; e.g. Sen. 9, 28, canorum illud in voce splendescit etiam in senectute. Cf. the metaph. uses of effulgere, emicare, enitere.
: cf. Tac. H. ii 1, Titi ingenium quantaecumque fortunae capax, decor oris cum quadam maiestate.
: see on c. 7, 2.
: so Nero is described as “ventre proiecto” (Ner. 51). Persius uses protensus, i 57, pinguis aqualiculus (“paunch'') protenso sesquipede extet.

: this is the reading of nQ; the other MSS. have memoriae, but the nom. is required. Oudendorp suggested memoria et singularis docilitas. The whole passage very closely resembles the description of Germanicus in Calig. 3, 1, Omnes Germanico corporis animique virtutes, et quantas nemini cuiquam, contigisse satis constat: formam et fortitudinem egregiam, ingenium in utroque eloquentiae doctrinaeque genere praecellens, benivolentiam singularem conciliandaeque hominum gratiae ac promerendi amoris mirum et efficax studium.

: Suet. extends to the subst. the constr. often found with the adj., e.g. Calig. 54, 2, docilis ad cetera. In class. Lat. docilis is used either abs. or c. ad; in poetry at times c. gen.; in post-Aug. writers at times c. abl.

: it was exceptional to excel in both; cf. Hom. Il. xiii 730, ἄλλῳ μὲν γὰρ ἔδωκε θεὸς πολεμήϊα ἔργα, κ.τ.λ. : Prop. iii 9, 19, hic satus ad pacem, hic castrensibus utilis armis: Plin. Pan. 4, Enituit aliquis in bello, sed obsolevit in paсе. Alium toga, sed non et arma honestarunt: Claud. Laud. Stil. i 27, bellis insignior ille, Sed pacem foedat vitiis Partitum; singula quemque Nobilitant. Titus was like Scipio Aemilianus, whom Velleius (i 12) describes as “omnibus belli ac togae dotibus ingenique ac studiorum eminentissimus saeculi sui.” ..

div.p: § 2. armorum et equitandi peritissimus: Suetonius uses the same words of Julius Caesar (Iul. 57).

p.note: : Eutrop. vii 21, facundissimus, bellicosissimus, moderatissimus; causas Latine egit, poemata et tragoedias Graece composuit: Suidas, τῇ μὲν Λατίνων ἐπιχωρίῳ γλώττῃ πρὸς τὰς τῶν κοινῶν ἐχρῆτο διοικήσεις, ποιήματα δὲ καὶ τραγῳδίας Ἑλλάδι φωνῇ διεπονεῖτο. Suidas also styles Titus εὐγλωττότατος (facundissimus).
: Quintilian (prooem. 4) uses ars orandi for the oratorical art. In Calig. 3, 2, Suetonius has orare causam (so Livy); cf. orare litem (Cic.).

: fingere (like πλάττειν) was used by the poets in the sense of composing; e.g. Hor. C. iv 2, 31, operosa parvus Carmina fingo. Pliny (N.H., praef. 5) eulogizes the eloquence and poetic skill of Titus: Fulgurat in ullo umquam verius dicta vis eloquentiae, tribuniciae potestatis facundia? Quanto tu ore patris laudes tonas! quanto fratris amas! quantus in poetica es! O magna fecunditas animi!
: the position of usque varies; cf. Vesp. 24, usque ad defectionem: Tib. 51, 1, ad simultatem usque processit: Galb. 19, 2, in Forum usque: Tib. 2, 4, usque in Capitolium.

: Suetonius seems to have coined this subst. to express what he elsewhere calls "ad subita extemporalis facultas'' (Aug. 84, 1). The adj. extemporalis is common in post-Aug. writers (Quintil., Plin. Ep., Mart., Tac., etc.); Cicero uses subito dicere and subita et fortuita oratio (de or. i 33, 150); also ex tempore, e.g. Arch. 8, 18, magnum numerum optimorum versuum dicere ex tempore: de or. iii 50, 194, versus fundere ex tempore.

: Friedlaender (Sitteng. ii10 183 sqq.) traces the modifying influence of Greek manners and customs on the old Roman prejudice not merely against professional but also against amateur musicians. Nepos (Epam. 1) states bluntly the old point of view that music was unseemly for a man of prominent position: musicen nostris moribus abesse a principis persona. Under the Empire musical dilettantism was very widespread even in the highest circles. Nero, Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, Alexander Severus, Elagabalus, Caracalla were among the emperors who cultivated the art.

: psallere was specially used of playing on the cithara (κυρίως ψάλλειν τὸ τῷ ἄκρῳ τῶν δακτύλων τῶν χορδῶν ἅπτεσθαι, Suidas), e.g. Hor. C. iv 13, 7, docta psallere Chia. We frequently find psallere joined with cantare or canere (e.g. Cic. Cat. ii 10, qui non solum cantare et psallere, sed etiam sicas vibrare didicerunt), and psallere itself was used of singing to the harp (cf. "psalm''). scienter: an adverb often used of a skilful musical performance; cf. Cic. Brut. 54, ex nervorum sono in fidibus quam scienter ei pulsi sint, intellegi solet: Nepos (praef. 1), saltasse eum (Epaminondam) commode, scienterque tibiis cantasse. Terence (Eun. 133) has the phrase scire fidibus "to be skilled on the lyre"; so too scitus is used with the gen. of the instrument played on, e.g. Ov. F. v 54, scita Thalia lyrae.

: notae (σημεῖα) = “shorthand'; notarius (σημειογράφος, ταχυγράφος) = 'shorthand writer." The signs used in shorthand at Rome were known as Notae Tironis, from Tiro the freedman and secretary of Cicero. For such contractions in MSS. see Lindsay, Introd. to Lat. Text. Emend. p. 91. Cato's speech against Caesar on the subject of the Catilinarian conspiracy was the first speech in the senate reported in shorthand. system was developed and augmented by Maecenas and Seneca. Tiro's

: in the epigram (146) of Ausonius entitled "Ad Notarium Velocissime Excipientem'' the speed of the notarius is described in an exaggerated fashion: Tu sensa nostri pectoris | ut dicta iam ceris tenes |... Tu me loquentem praevenis. | Quis, quaeso, quis me prodidit? | Quis ista iam dixit tibi, | quae cogitabam dicere? Cf. Mart. xiv 208, Currant verba licet, manus est velocior illis; | nondum lingua suum, dextra peregit opus: Manil. iv 197, Ille scriptor erit felix, cui littera verbum est, | quique notis linguam superet cursumque loquentis, | excipiens longas nova per compendia voces: Sen. Ep. 90, 25, Quid (loquar) verborum notas, quibus quamvis citata excipitur oratio et celeritatem linguae manus sequitur?

: the subst. amanuensis is first found in Suetonius, who uses it also in Ner. 44, 1. It denotes a secretary, a confidential slave or freedman, servus a manu; cf. Aug. 67, 2, Thallo a manu, quod pro epistula prodita denarios quingentos accepisset, crura ei fregit: Iul. 74, 1, Philemon a manu: Vesp. 3, Caenis, Antoniae liberta et a manu. Another phrase is ab epistulis; e.g. Claud. 28, Narcissus ab epistulis, Pallas a rationibus.

: chirographum (χειρόγραφον), first used by Cicero, has three meanings in Suetonius: (1) handwriting (as here; Aug. 64, 3, ut imitarentur chirographum suum; Ner. 52, versibus ipsius chirographo scriptis): (2) a letter or document in a person's handwriting (as Tit. 6, 2, chirographum eius praeparatae apud milites contionis, Aug. 87, 3,; Dom. 1, 1; Iul. 17, 1; Calig. 24, 3): (3) a bond (cautio) under one's own hand, guaranteeing the fulfilment of an obligation (Calig. 12, 2, deque ea re et iure iurando et chirographo cavit).

: falsarius is found once earlier in Cato (or. inc. frag. 28, Meyer) of one who is guilty of “suppressio veri”: Tu, inquam, si verum supprimis, falsarius agnosceris; si falsa confingis, mendax esse videris.. In Suetonius and later writers it means a forger of written documents, especially wills. Precautions devised against falsarii in the reign of Nero are mentioned in Ner. 17: adversus falsarios tunc primum repertum, ne tabulae, nisi pertusae, ac ter lino per foramina traiecto, obsignarentur, etc. When a falsarius was convicted before Claudius, some one in court cried out that his hands should be cut off, whereupon the emperor at once ordered the executioner to be summoned with knife and butcher's block (Claud. 15, 2). Banishment and confiscation of goods were the penalties for forgery under the Lex Cornelia de falsis (81 B.c.) also known as the Lex testamentaria. Cicero uses testamentarius for a forger (Off. iii 73, Sest. 39). For Domitian's allegation that Titus falsified Vespasian's will see Dom. 2, 3.

: see on Vesp. 2, 3. Titus would be at least 20 when he was appointed tribune (Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 366), probably nearer 25 (Mommsen, Hermes iii 43). Military service, generally for a year, was a necessary preliminary to a senatorial career (Galb. 6, 1, n.); e.g. the younger Pliny served as military tribune in Syria (Plin. Ep. iii 11). See also on “praefectura,” Vesp. 8, 3.

: cf. the speech of Mucianus to Vespasian, Tac. H. ii 77: Tuae domui triumphale nomen, duo iuvenes, capax iam imperii alter (i.e. Titus) et primis militiae annis apud Germanicos quoque exercitus clarus. The statement made by Heraeus (on Tac. H. ii 1) and by Spooner (on H. ii 77) that Titus served as military tribune under his father Vespasian when he was in command of a legion in Germany (Vesp. 4, 1) is absurd. Vespasian got his command in Germany in 41/42 A.D., and Titus was born in 39 A.D. (41 A.D., according to Suet. Tit. 1). Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2697) erroneously says that Titus is given the title of “Germanicus" in Tac. H. iii 66, for the Germanicus mentioned there is a son of Vitellius. The elder Pliny, in the Preface to his N.H. (dedicated to Titus), refers to his having served in the army with Titus: et nobis quidem qualis (tu) in castrensi contubernio! Nothing definite is known as to when and where Pliny (born 23/24 A.D.) and Titus served together; for the theory that it was during the war in Judaea see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 51, Weynand l.c.

: Dio (1x 30) makes the statement, which is chronologically impossible, that Titus accompanied Vespasian to Britain in 43 A.D., and saved his father's life when he was sore pressed by the Britons in 47. See Furneaux, Tac. Ann. Vol. ii² p. 132 n. Vespasian's military achievements in Britain are mentioned in Vesp. 4, 1.
: his father was characterised by the same energetic discharge of military duties; cf. Vesp. 4, 5 delectus est ut industriae expertae.
: “disinterestedness,” “integrity'"; cf. the use of modestus (= ἐγκρατής) in Dom. 8, 2 of magistrates and provincial governors who refrain from extortion, etc.
: these presumably were set up after the establishment of the Flavian dynasty at Rome.
: inscriptions on the base ('basis,” Vesp. 23, 3) of statues and busts, giving the distinctions of the person represented; cf. Dom. 15, 2, Galb. 2.

div.p: §2. Foro operam dedit: at Rome under the Empire the forum Romanum, the forum (Iulii) Caesaris, and the forum Augusti were used for the trial of lawsuits; hence triplex forum in Mart. iii 38, 4, "Causas,” inquis, “agam Cicerone disertior ipso, | atque erit in triplici par mihi nemo foro.”

p.note: : Titus did not appear regularly in court, but only in cases where glory was to be won. Pliny (Ep. vi 29), after enumerating various kinds of cases which a pleader ought to undertake, says: "Ad haec ego genera causarum, ambitiose fortasse, addam tamen claras et inlustres. Aequum est enim agere ("to plead") поп numquam gloriae et famae, id est suam causam.”

: the correct form of this name was restored by Roth; the MSS. have adrecidiam (arr-, ПR). Arrecina Tertulla was the daughter of M. Arrecinus Clemens, who was praetorian prefect under Caligula in 41 A.D. (Tac. H. iv 68, Joseph. Ant. Iud. xix 37 sqq.). Her brother, M. Arrecinus Clemens, also was praetorian prefect and twice consul; see Dom. 11, 1. Arrecina Tertulla is twice mentioned in inscriptions: C.I.L. vi 12355 (Newton 234), Dis manibus M. Arrecini Melioris, Arrecina Tertulla delicio suo fecit. v(ixit) a(nnis) viii d(iebus) x: C.I.L. vi 12357 (Newton 235), D. m. Arrecinae Gnomes, Arrecina Tertulla delicio suo fecit.

: the highest office open to the equestrian order (summa equestris gradus, Galb. 14, 2; cf. Tit. 6, 1). In Republican days the praetoria cohors was the bodyguard attached to the general; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 223 Müll.: praetoria cohors est dicta quod a praetore non discedebat. Scipio enim Africanus primus fortissimum quemque delegit, qui ab eo in bello non discederent et cetero munere militiae vacarent et sesquiplex stipendium acciperent. Under Augustus there were 9 cohorts in different parts of Rome and in the places in Italy where he usually stayed. Each cohort consisted of 1000 men (10 centuries) and 10 turmae of cavalry. Sejanus, under Tiberius, concentrated the cohorts Their in a camp outside the Viminal gate of Rome (Galb. 19, 1, n.). They were increased to 11 or 12 under Caligula or Claudius. Vitellius disbanded them (Vitell. 10, 1), but later enrolled 16 new cohorts. The number was reduced to 9 by Vespasian, and was subsequently fixed at 10. supreme commander was the emperor, but he delegated his command, usually to 2 praefecti praetorio (-ii), sometimes to 1, after the time of Commodus to 3. Suetonius uses praefectus praetorii in Galb. 11:14, 2: Claud. 12, 1: Ner. 21, 1: Calig. 56, 1; praefectus (sc. praetorii) in Calig. 23, 2: Claud. 21, 3: Ner. 35, 5. The designation praefectus cohortium praetorianarum used here and in Dom. 6, 1 is irregular. Though writers at times use cohortes praetorianae, the regular phrase in inscriptions, especially military diplomata, is cohortes praetoriae. See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 866 sqq.

: daughter of the Antonia Furnilla, wife of Q. Marcius Barea Sura, who is mentioned in an inscription at Rome (Dessau, 953): Antonia A. f. Furnilla Q. Marcii Q. f. C. n., C. et Gemini Artori pronepotis, Bareae Surae.
: see on Oth. 1, 3.

: tollere was used of the father taking up and acknowledging as his the new-born child which was laid at his feet, and so tollere liberos = procreare, gignere; cf. Ner. 5, 2, sublato filio Nerone ex Agrippina: Tib. 7, 2, sublato ex ea filio Druso: Cic. Phil. xiii 10, qui ex Fadia sustulerit liberos.

: named Julia. She was born before 67, and Jerusalem was taken by Titus on her birthday in 70 (see c. 5, 2). She received the title "Augusta" in her father's reign, and is so styled on coins of Titus with the legend Iulia Augusta T(iti) Aug(usti) f(ilia) or Iulia Imp. T. Aug. f. Augusta (Eckhel, vi p. 367; Cohen, i² p. 465 sq.). After being offered in marriage to Domitian, who refused her (Dom. 22), she wedded her cousin Flavius Sabinus. When he was put to death by Domitian's orders (Dom. 10, 4), Domitian, who was separated at the time from his wife Domitia, lived with Julia as with a wife, and even after he took back Domitia (Dom. 3, 1) he continued his illicit relations with his niece, and was the cause of her death through abortion (Dom. 22). She died before 90 A.D., as she is called diva on a coin of that year (see Friedlaender, Mart. Introd. p. 57). Martial (vi 3 and 13) writes of her as already deified, that book of his epigrams being published in 90. Her name appears in the vow of the Fratres Arvales for the safety of the imperial family, January 3, 87 (C.I.L. vi 2065), but is omitted in the vow of January 3, 90 (C.I.L. vi 2067), so that presumably she died before the latter date (see Newton, op. cit. p. 101).

div.p: § 3. quaesturae: the minimum age for the quaestorship was 25; presumably Titus was quaestor in 64 or 65.

p.note: : when Vespasian was appointed by Nero in the winter 66/67 to conduct the war in Judaea (see Vesp. 4, 5), he sent Titus to Alexandria to lead as legatus the 15th legion (Apollinaris) from there to Judaea. Vespasian went from Achaea overland via the Hellespont, and was joined by Titus at Ptolemais (Acre) on the coast of Phoenicia (Joseph. Bell. Iud. iii 8, 64).

: read by Ursinus, Roth, Preud'homme: Tarichias, Bentley; Tarichaeas, Ihm; Taricheam, Herm. Barbarus; the MSS. have thracias (thacias, G; trachias, Πк). The city of Taricheae (Ταριχέαι, Strab.; Ταριχαῖαι, Joseph.; Tarichea, Plin. N.H.) was in Galilee on the western side of the sea or lake of Tiberias (Gennesaret). Strabo (xvi 764) says it got its name from the fish-curing industry (ἡ λίμνη ταριχείας ἰχθύων ἀστείας παρέχει). It was fortified by Josephus who made it his headquarters in the rebellion of the Jews against Rome. It was taken by Titus with great slaughter (Joseph. Bell. Iud. iii 485 sqq.).

: opposite Taricheae, on the eastern side of the lake. Built on a precipitous hill resembling a camel's hump (hence the name), it too was strongly fortified by Josephus and fiercely defended by the Zealots against Vespasian. Titus, who had been sent on a mission to Mucianus, the legatus of Syria, found on his return that Vesp. had been beaten back from Gamala. At the head of a small body of picked troops Titus forced his way into the city and Vesp. sent back his whole army to support him. The city was captured during a violent storm and 9000 of the inhabitants perished (Joseph. iv 1 sqq.). Titus also effected the capture of Gischala, and with its downfall the conquest of Galilee was complete. sunt

: cf. Coel. or. frag. 3 (Paul. ex Fest. p. 182 M.), equusque mihi sub feminibus occisus erat. Isidorus (Orig. 11, 1, 106) mentions the phrase in his attempt to differentiate between femora and femina: "femora” ab inguinibus usque ad genua, “femina” autem per derivationem femorum partes sunt, quibus in equitando tergis equorum adhaeremus; unde et proeliatores olim sub feminibus equos amisisse dicebantur. Formations from femin- are much more frequent than those from femor- in the plur. of femur (femen); see statistics in Thes. Ling. Lat. Suetonius uses femur, femore, femina, feminibus.
: Suet. also has the more usual conscendere equum, ascendere equum (in equum, Cic.). less.

: "rider," as in Tac. and Sil. Ital.; vector (Heinsius) is needcirca se: "by his side." For se instead of eum see on Vesp. 15, 1, qui se salutaverat. The use of circa is the same as in Claud. 36, quodam cum ferro circa sacrificantem se deprehenso. Suetonius uses circa very freely in the spatial sense of prope (in c. 9, 2 = utrubique "on both sides of'"); he also has it of those who are about a person, his suite, associates, etc. (cf. οἱ περί τινα); e.g. Dom. 9, 2, omnes circa se largissime prosecutus. See also on Oth. 11, circa lucem: Dom. 3, 2, circa administrationem imperii. The late variant contra se is adopted by most of the early editors (not by Oudendorp, Wolf, or Bremi), with the view of enhancing the valour of Titus.

: he was sent by Vespasian; cf. Tac. H. i 10, nec Vespasiano adversus Galbam votum aut animus: quippe Titum filium ad venerationem cultumque eius miserat: H. ii 1, Titus Vespasianus e Iudaea, incolumi adhuc Galba, missus a patre. Josephus (Bell. Iud. iv 498) says that king Agrippa went from Judaea along with Titus to pay homage to Galba; he also says that Vespasian wished to receive directions from Galba with regard to the war in Judaea. In Gall. 23 Suetonius mentions Vespasian's belief that Galba had sent emissaries from Spain to Judaea to assassinate him.

: quaqua (= quacumque or quocumque) is ante- and post-class.; e.g. Plaut. Mil. 92, quaqua incedit: Apul. Met. xi 4, quaqua perfluebat. Cf. Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre ii 635. For the use of the subjunctive see App. i § 8. b. (2).
: see on Vesp. 4, 6. .. ..

: quasi is widely used in Silver Lat. in a causal sense. The cause or reason introduced by quasi is often purely subjective, but there is no necessary implication of falsehood. Suetonius has it (a) with the subjunctive as here and in Dom. 10, 4, occidit Helvidium, quasi taxasset: Vesp. 6, 2, perseveraverunt, quasi rumori minus crederent: Aug. 11, medicus custoditus, quasi venenum volneri indidisset; (b) with nouns, adjs., ptcples.; e.g. Oth. 1, 2, praepositos suos, quasi defectionis auctores, occiderant : Galb. 3, 4, ne quasi ignaram fallere videretur: Aug. 86, 2, increpat Antonium, quasi scribentem ea. For examples in other authors see Kühner-Stegmann, ii 456.

: Tac. H. ii 1, Titus causam profectionis officium erga principem (i.e. Galba) et maturam petendis honoribus iuventam ferebat ("alleged"), sed vulgus fingendi avidum disperserat accitum in adoptionem. Materia sermonibus senium et orbitas principis et intemperantia ('impatience'") civitatis, donec unus eligatur, multos destinandi. Galba's choice of an adopted son and successor see Galb. 17. .. For

: the considerations which influenced Titus in deciding whether he should return, or continue his journey to Rome, are described by Tac. (l.c.): Ubi Corinthi certos nuntios accepit de interitu Galbae et aderant qui arma Vitellii bellumque affirmarent, anxius animo paucis amicorum adhibitis cuncta utrimque perlustrat. Si pergeret in urbem nullam officii gratiam in alterius honorem suscepti ac se Vitellio sive Othoni obsidem fore: sin rediret, offensam haud dubiam victoris, sed incerta adhuc victoria et concedente in partes patre filium excusatum. Sin Vespasianus rem publicam susciperet, obliviscendum offensarum de bello agitantibus. His ac talibus inter spem metumque iactatum spes vicit. This is the only passage in which Suetonius uses ubi in a temporal sense.

: perf. Tacitus (H. ii 2) describes his return journey from Corinth. He coasted along Achaea (Attica and Euboea) and then sailed across the Aegaean to Asia Minor, and descending that coast and leaving it on the left, he arrived at Rhodes and Cyprus. From Cyprus he sailed by a bolder course (audentioribus spatiis) across the open sea to Syria. adito Paphiae Veneris oraculo: Tac. (l.c.), Atque illum cupido incessit adeundi visendique templum Paphiae Veneris inclitum per indigenas advenasque. The foundation of this famous temple and oracle at Paphos in Cyprus, where Aphrodite was said to have landed when she rose from the sea, is discussed by Tacitus (H. ii 3, cf. A. iii 62). The image of the goddess was merely a cone-shaped stone, and the altar, though in the open air, was never wet by rain. Pausanias (i 14) says that her worship was introduced at Paphos from Assyria, but more probably it was Phoenician colonists who spread the cult of Venus Urania (= Astarte); cf. Hdt. i 105. A grove and altar of Aphrodite at Paphos are mentioned in Hom. Od. viii 362. One of the functions of the sea-born goddess was to grant to mariners a favourable voyage; hence such titles of hers as Εὔπλοια (Roscher, Lex. Myth. i 402).

: Tac. H. ii 5, Titus de navigatione primum consuluit. Postquam pandi viam et mare prosperum accepit, de se per ambages interrogat caesis compluribus hostiis. Sostratus (sacerdotis id nomen erat) ubi laeta et congruentia exta magnisque consultis adnuere deam videt, pauca in praesens et solita respondens petito secreto futura aperit. Titus aucto animo ad patrem pervectus suspensis provinciarum et exercituum mentibus ingens rerum fiducia accessit.
: like Vespasian, when he consulted the oracle of the god of Carmel, Vesp. 5, 6; cf. also Galb. 9, 2.

div.p: §2. cuius brevi compos: cuius refers to spe; cf. Liv. xxix 22, spei conceptae compos: Suet. Aug. 28, 2, fecit ipse se compotem voti: Aug. 58, 2, compos factus votorum meorum: Romanum voti compotem fecit. Calig. 13, imperium adeptus populum The hopes of Titus were as good as realised when his father Vespasian was chosen as emperor.

p.note: : cf. Tac. H. v 1, eiusdem anni (70 A.D.) principio Caesar Titus perdomandae Iudaeae delectus a patre: Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, Iudaeique (in pacem coacti) annitente filio Tito, quem transgrediens in Italiam reliquerat externae militiae: Oros. vii 9, relictoque in castris ad procurationem obsidionis Hierosolymorum filio Tito: Joseph. Bell. Iud. iv 658, κατὰ τάχος τὰ κατὰ τὴν ᾿Αλεξάνδρειαν διώκει (Οὐεσπασιανός) τὸν δ' υἱὸν Τίτον μετὰ τῆς ἐκκρίτου δυνάμεως ἀπέστειλεν ἐξαιρήσοντα Ἱεροσόλυμα. Vespasian was proclaimed emperor by the legions in Egypt, Judaea, and Syria in July, 69 (Vesp. 6, 3). Towards the close of that year he went to Alexandria along with Titus. Before setting out for Italy he made arrangements for the occupation of Egypt, so that he could cut off the corn-supply of Rome and compel Vitellius to surrender by famine (Tac. H. iii 48). Titus was sent back to Palestine to conduct the siege of Jerusalem.

: the name Ἱεροσόλυμα (Hierosolyma) for Jerusalem seems to occur first in Hecataeus of Abdera, a contemporary of Alexander the Great. It is used in the Apocrypha, while the form generally found in the Septuagint is Ἱερουσαλήμ. The name Ἱεροσόλυμα was explained as ἱερὸν Σολύμων, and this gave rise to the belief that the Jews were identical with the Solymi (ancient dwellers in Lycia, mentioned by Homer and Herodotus); cf. Tac. H. v 2, clara alii Iudaeorum initia, Solymos, carminibus Homeri celebratam gentem, conditae urbi Hierosolyma nomen e suo fecisse. ..

: Joseph. v 288, δώδεκα αὐτὸς τῶν προμάχων ἀναιρεῖ: Eutrop. vii 21, 2, in oppugnatione Hierosolymorum sub patre militans duodecim propugnatores duodecim sagittarum confixit ictibus. cepit: the siege of Jerusalem by Titus began in the spring of 70 A.D. and lasted over five months. The Temple with its treasures was destroyed by fire, probably on Aug. 6, and on Sept. 2 the upper city, where the last resistance was offered, was stormed by the Romans (Joseph. vi 260 sqq., 393 sqq.).
: this is the reading of M; the other MSS. have eam (sc. urbem, to be supplied κατὰ σύνεσιν from Hierosolymorum).
: Julia; see on c. 4, 2.

: Oros. vii 9, 6, Titus imperator ab exercitu pronuntiatus: Joseph. vi 316, τὸν Τίτον μετὰ μεγίστων εὐφημιῶν ἀπέφηναν αὐτοκράτορα (Joseph. says that this salutation by the soldiers took place after the burning of the Temple). The title imperator (αὐτοκράτωρ) was given by acclamation on the field of battle; e.g. Caes. B.C. ii 26, Curio.. universi exercitus conclamatione imperator appellatur. The earliest example is that of Scipio Africanus (209 B.c., Liv. xxvii 19). The last occasion on which the honour of being acclaimed imperator was granted to a private person was in 22 A.D., when Tiberius allowed it to Junius Blaesus, proconsul of Africa; Tac. A. iii 74, Tiberius Blaeso tribuit ut imperator a legionibus salutaretur prisco erga duces honore, qui bene gesta re publica gaudio et impetu victoris exercitus conclamabantur... Concessit quibusdam et Augustus id vocabulum, ac tunc Tiberius Blaeso postremum. The Emperors were saluted in this way for victories gained either by themselves or by their lieutenants (legati), and the number of these salutations appeared in the list of their titles. = In

: atque etiam, "and even"; cf. Calig. 40. In other passages Suetonius uses nec non et merely as a copula ("and also") connecting individual terms or concepts (Vesp. 8, 2:18: Dom. 14, 1). poetry and late prose nec non et is frequently used to connect sentences (not individual words); e.g. Verg. G. ii 53, Aen. i 748, viii 461: Colum. viii 15, 6: Plin. N.H. vii 183, etc.: Quintil. ix 4, 25, etc. See KühnerStegmann, i 826 sq., on this and other combinations such as nec non etiam, nec non .. quoque, nec non et quoque. ..

: Titus did not yield to the solicitations of the troops. He broke up his army when his task in Judaea was accomplished. The 12th legion was sent back to Melitene on the Euphrates; the 10th was left in Jerusalem; the 5th and 15th accompanied him to the various cities which he visited in the eight months which elapsed before he returned to Rome. Before setting out on his homeward voyage from Alexandria he sent back these two legions to their earlier quarters, the 5th to Moesia and the 15th to Pannonia (Joseph. B.I. vii 18–20, 117).

div.p: § 3. suspicio quasi temptasset: in post-Aug. writers quasi c. subj. is used for the acc. c. inf. with verbs of saying, believing, accusing, etc., as well as with nouns such as fama, rumor, opinio, suspicio, the clause with quasi having a strong subjective colouring (cf. Kühner-Stegmann, ii 456). Suetonius uses this constr. freely; e.g. Tit. 8, 1, admonentibus domesticis, quasi plura polliceretur quam praestare posset: Tib. 21, 2, scio vulgo persuasum, quasi vox Augusti per cubicularios excepta sit: Aug. 94, 8, somnium aliter exponunt, quasi Iuppiter demonstrasset: Aug. 28, 1, obiectum sibi ab eo saepius, quasi per ipsum staret ne redderetur (res publica): Dom. 22, erat fama, quasi develleret: Aug. 14, rumore dilato, quasi necasset: Aug. 6, concepta opinione veteri, quasi temere adeuntibus horror quidam et metus obiciatur. For similar uses of tamquam see on Vitell. 16. ..

p.note: : when Jerusalem had been captured, Titus went down to Caesarea on the sea. He was hindered from undertaking the voyage to Rome immediately, as it was the winter season (70/71 A.D.). He held celebrations of various kinds at Caesarea on the sea, Caesarea Philippi, Berytus, and the cities of Syria. He then went by Antiochia to Zeugma on the Euphrates, where he received an embassy from the Parthian king Vologaesus (Vesp. 6, 4) who presented him with a golden crown for his victory in Judaea. Finally, he set out for Egypt, visiting the ruins of Jerusalem on his journey, and arrived at Alexandria at the beginning of May, 71. There he embarked for Italy.
: the oldest capital of Egypt, about 15 miles south of Cairo, on the western bank of the Nile.

: Apis ("Απις, Egyptian Hapi "the hidden") was a sacred bull worshipped with the greatest reverence by the Egyptians at Memphis (Hdt. iii 27-29; Plut. Is. et Osir. 20, 29, 43, etc.; Lucian de sacrif. 15; Pomp. Mel. i 9). He was regarded as the incarnation of the god Ptah, or of Osiris, or of the Sun, and was connected with the river-god Nilus. Fire was said to come down from heaven upon the cow, which thereupon conceives Apis. The calf which is so called is black with a square spot of white upon his forehead, and on his back the figure of an eagle; the hairs in his tail are double, and there is a scarab or beetle upon his tongue (Hdt. iii 28). The ceremony of consecrating the new-born bull is described in Ael. Hist. An. xi 10, Diod. Sic. i 85, Plin. N.H. viii 71, Amm. Marc. xxii 14. He was not allowed to live for more than 25 years. If he died before that age, he was splendidly entombed in a chamber under the temple of Serapis at Memphis which was called the Serapeum. After death he became Osiris-Apis (Osir-Hapi), the most probable origin of the name Serapis (Sarapis); see on Vesp. 7, 1.

: the wearing of a diadem suggested regal aspirations. In its most general sense diadema was a synonym of taenia, vitta, fascia, stemma, strophium, mitra, and the other Gr. and Lat. words denoting a band encircling the head (Daremberg-Saglio, ii 119). It was used for the band round the brow of priests and celebrants of religious rites. As a symbol of sovereignty it was worn by Assyrian and Persian kings, by Alexander (after his conquest of Darius), by the Diadochi, etc. The diadema as a regni insigne (Cic. Ph. iii 5) was hated by the Romans and refused by Caesar (Suet. Iul. 79, where it is described as a white band, fascia candida). Caligula thought of assuming it and establishing a regnum or absolute monarchy (Calig. 22, 1). In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 35 we are told that Aurelianus (270-275) was the first Roman emperor to wear a diadem; but the first represented with it on coins is Constantine (306-337). •

: a comparative of the adv. secus (Tit. 11, Galb. 14, 1) from sequor, lit. "following" "not attaining to" and so "inferior” “worse''; cf. Tib. 2, 1, multa egregia merita, multa etiam sequius admissa in rem p. extant. The form sequius is found first in Afran. 293 R., sin, id quod non spero, ratio talis sequius ceciderit; it does not occur in class. Lat. though secus does (e.g. Cic. Att. vi 2, 2, ne quid fiat secus quam volumus), but is fairly common from Livy on. Distinguish sētius, which is joined with non, nec, neque, nihilo, eo, and quo, and is equivalent to minus (e.g. Vesp. 6, 2: Dom. 2, 2: Vitell. 10, 3). It is very doubtful whether setius is connected with secus and sequius, though the Roman grammarians regarded it as a byform of sequius; see Lindsay, Lat. Lang. 566: Zimmermann, Archiv Lexik. iv 604.
: a town in the extreme S.W. of Italy on the Sicilian strait, mod. Reggio di Calabria.

: see on Vitell. 12. inopinanti patri: Josephus (B.I. vii 119) says that his father was expecting Titus and went forth to welcome him: τοῦ πλοῦ δ᾽ αὐτῷ κατὰ νοῦν ἀνυσθέντος, ὁμοίως μὲν ἡ ῾Ρώμη περὶ τὴν ὑποδοχὴν εἶχε καὶ τὰς ὑπαντήσεις ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ πατρός, λαμπρότερον δ᾽ ἦν Τίτῳ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ πατὴρ ὑπαντῶν καὶ δεχόμενος. =
: redarguens, refellens, refutans; cf. Tac. A. iv 11, mihi tradendi arguendique rumoris causa fuit, ut claro sub exemplo falsas auditiones depellerem. This use of arguere is not found before Livy.
: the canards that he would not return to Italy, but would found a new kingdom in the East.

: = vanitatem "groundlessness” “idleness"; cf. Dom. 15, 3, ad coarguendam temeritatem artis (mathematicae). The relations between Titus and Vespasian are examined exhaustively by Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2706 sqq.), and he shows that there is not the smallest reason to assume any want of loyalty on the part of Titus towards his father, or the existence of any friction between them. In the interview which, according to Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vi 30), took place at Tarsus between Titus and Apollonius of Tyana, the philosopher Apollonius congratulates Titus on his readiness to subordinate himself in all things to his father and to render him homage. = ..

: so Tacitus (H. ii 83) describes Mucianus as “socium magis imperii quam ministrum agens." For agere in the sense of agere partes cf. Claud. 29, 1, non principem sed ministrum egit: Tib. 12, 2, obnoxium et trepidum agit: 26, 2, privatum egit. Distinguish agere se gerere se "to pass oneself off as"; Claud. 25, 1, libertini, qui se pro equitibus R. agerent. For the position of the particeps (consors) imperii in relation to the Princeps see on Tit. 9, 3, consortem successoremque. Titus returned to Rome ἰσομοιρήσων τῆς ἀρχῆς τῷ πατρί (Philostr. l.c.). Bury (Stud. Rom. Emp. p. 377) says: “Vespasian followed the example of Augustus and the more recent example of Galba, in taking to himself a consort in the Empire. Both the proconsular imperium and the tribunician power were conferred on his son Titus at the same time, and thus Titus held a position like that which Tiberius held in the last years of Augustus. The object of Vespasian was not to lighten his own labours, but to secure the succession for his son. Titus was allowed to assume more of the imperial privileges than had been conceded to any consort before. He wore the laurel wreath and vota were offered in his name. He also styled himself Imperator; but while Vespasian used this title as a praenomen, Titus bore it as a cognomen (Titus Caesar Imperator Vespasianus)." The difficulties connected with the varying application of the title Imperator to Titus on coins and in inscriptions during his father's reign are discussed by Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2708 sqq.); Schiller, Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit i 508; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 1154. 21 ..
: see Vesp. 8, 1 (notes).

: marking him as Vespasian's successor. The tribunicia potestas had previously been shared by Augustus, first with Agrippa and then with Tiberius, and by Tiberius with Drusus; cf. Tac. A. iii 56, Tiberius mittit litteras ad senatum, queis potestatem tribuniciam Druso petebat. Id summi fastigii vocabulum Augustus repperit, ne regis aut dictatoris nomen adsumeret ac tamen appellatione aliqua cetera imperia praemineret. Marcum deinde Agrippam socium eius potestatis, quo defuncto Tiberium Neronem delegit, ne successor in incerto foret. See also on Vesp. 12.

: in 70, 72, 74-77, 79 A.D.; cf. Vesp. 8, 1. Pliny (N.H. praef. 3), addressing Titus, says: Triumphalis et censorius tu, sexiesque consul, ac tribuniciae potestatis particeps: et quod his nobilius fecisti dum illud patri pariter et equestri ordini praestas, praefectus praetorio eius. Pliny's work was published in 77 A.D. orationes in senatu recitaret: Vespasian used both his sons (Titus and Domitian) for this purpose according to Dio lxvi 10, ὅσα μὴ ἐδύνατο αὐτὸς ὑπὸ τοῦ γήρως ἀναλέγεσθαι, ἢ καὶ ὅσα ἀπὼν ἐπέστελλε τῇ βουλῇ, διὰ τῶν υἱέων αὐτοῦ ὡς τὸ πολὺ ἐκέλευεν ἀναγιγνώσκεσθαι, τιμῶν κὰν τούτῳ αὐτήν. For orationes see on Dom. 2, 3.

: the principal duty of those quaestors who were nominated by the emperor (quaestores Caesaris, see on Vitell. 1, 2) was to read to the senate communications from him; cf. Aug. 65, 2, libello per quaestorem recitato notum senatui fecit: Dio liv 25, τὸ βιβλίον τῷ ταμίᾳ (quaestori) ἀναγνῶναι δούς : Tac. A. xvi 27, oratio principis per quaestorem eius audita est. Nero departed from the usual custom; Suet. Ner. 15, 2, orationes ad senatum missas, praeterito quaestorum officio, per consulem plerumque recitabat. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 569.

: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, 10, (Titum) victorem praefectura praetorio extulerat (Vespasianus). Unde etiam is honos, ingens a principio, tumidior atque alter ab Augusto imperio fuit. For an account of this office see on c. 4, 2. Suetonius is inaccurate in saying that Titus was the first prefect who was not an eques, for Arrecinus Clemens (see Dom. 11, 1), who was appointed by Mucianus before the arrival of Vespasian in Rome in the autumn of 70, was a senator; Tac. H. iv 68 Arrecinum Clementem praetorianis praeposuit, dictitans ipsum, quamquam senatorii ordinis, ad utraque munia (i.e. the duties of senator and prefect) sufficere. Augustus had followed the advice of Maecenas in ordaining that these prefects should be equites. M. Aurelius lamented that he could not make Pertinax praefectus praetorii because he was a senator (Capitol. Pert. 2). Alexander Severus made it his practice to promote his prefects of the guard to the rank of senator, in order that they might belong to the class of Viri Clarissimi and be so addressed (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 21). .. egit: sc. praefecturam; cf. Tib. 24, 1, principatum agere.
: cf. Flor. i 26, altius se et incivilius efferens. See note on "civile,” Vesp. 9, 2. incivilis and inciviliter are post-class.

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 4, praefecturam praetorianam patre imperante adeptus, suspectum quemque et oppositum sibi, immissis, qui per theatra et castris invidiosa iactantes ad poenam poscerent, quasi criminis convictos oppressit. Suetonius uses summittere in the sense of sending secretly, e.g. Galb. 23; also in the sense of suborning (subornare, ὑφιέναι), e.g. Ner. 28, 1, Acten libertam paulum afuit quin iusto sibi matrimonio coniungeret, summissis consularibus viris qui regio genere ortam peierarent.

: in the theatres and circus the people, accustomed to call for their favourite actors and gladiators, often indulged in outbursts of political feeling and clamorously demanded reforms, executions, etc. Cicero mentions such demonstrations in his day (e.g. Att. i 16, Sest. 54, 115); and under the Empire, when public assemblies were abolished, the gatherings of the people in the theatres and at other shows became the regular occasions of giving expression to public demands. Cf. Dom. 13, 1; Тас. Н. i 32, 72; A. vi 13. Tiberius avoided the shows on account of this licence: Tib. 47, Neque spectacula omnino edidit; et iis quae ab aliquo ederentur rarissime interfuit, ne quid exposceretur. See Hardy on Plut. Galb. 17, & ῾Ῥωμαίων δῆμος . ἐν πᾶσι θεάτροις καὶ σταδίοις αἰτούμενος ἐκεῖνον (i.e. demanding the execution of Tigellinus; cf. Suet. Galb. 15, 2).

div.p: §2. Aulum Caecinam: Aulus Caecina Alienus was quaestor in Hispania Baetica in 68 A.D., the year of Nero's death. He was one of the first to side with Galba, who gave him the command of a legion in Upper Germany; but shortly afterwards Galba ordered his prosecution for peculation, and Caecina, to be revenged, induced his troops to declare for Vitellius (Tac. H. i 53). He was chosen general by Vitellius and led an army into Italy, taking part in the battle of Betriacum. When Vitellius took possession of Rome, Caecina was made consul (Sept. 1, 69). Later he was sent by Vitellius to meet Antonius Primus and the Flavian forces, but he proved a traitor (see note on “proditus,” Vitell. 15, 2). (lxvi 16) agrees with Suetonius that Titus had Caecina assassinated on account of his revolutionary designs against Vespasian: 'Αλιηνὸς μὲν αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ βασιλείῳ, ἐξαναστὰς ἐκ τοῦ συσσιτίου, εὐθὺς ἀπεσφάγη, τοῦ Τίτου κελεύσαντος, μὴ καὶ φθάσῃ τι τῆς νυκτός νεοχμῶσαι· τῶν γὰρ στρατιωτῶν συχνοὺς προπαρεσκεύαστο. In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 4 a different reason is assigned: Caecinam consularem adhibitum cenae, vixdum triclinio egressum, ob suspicionem stupratae Berenices uxoris suae iugulari iussit.

p.note: : see on c. 3, 2. Dio
: sc. habendae. Cf. Tac. Dial. 41, quid opus est multis apud populum contionibus? The variant coniurationis has been generally rejected since Casaubon's ed.

: cf. Vesp. 4, 4, gravissimam contraxit offensam: Sen. Ep. 87, 31, divitiae neu invidiam contrahunt: Curt. viii 5, invidiam tali adulatione contraheres: Justin v 2, sed apud Lacedaemonios virtus Alcibiadis plus invidiae quam gratiae contraxit.

: from meaning "not lightly or casually” “not without good reason” (Gr. οὐκ ἐτός), non temere came to be used in the sense of non facile, vix, hardly” “scarcely” (Germ. nicht leicht). This occurs e.g. in Cic. Q. Fratr. i 1, 13, Caes. B.G. iv 20, Nep. Att. 20, Liv. ii 61, 4. See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 587. Suetonius uses non temere in this way over twenty times, e.g. Tit. 8, 3; Dom. 19 and 21; Vesp. 15.

: the opposite phrase secundo rumore is as old as Ennius (Ann. 262, populi rumore secundo). Livy and Tacitus use esse adverso rumore (abl. of quality); e.g. Liv. xxvii 20, Romae Marcellus etiam adverso rumore esse: Tac. A. xiv 11, sed adverso rumore Seneca erat, 212 quod oratione tali confessionem scripsisset: H. ii 26, apud paucos ea ducis ratio probata, in vulgus adverso rumore fuit; cf. Suet. Iul. 2, secundiore fama fuit.

: cf. the description of the youthful Nero, Ner. 26, 1, petulantiam, libidinem, luxuriam, avaritiam, crudelitatem sensim quidem primo et occulte et velut iuvenili errore exercuit, sed ut tunc quoque dubium nemini foret naturae illa vitia, non aetatis esse.
: cf. Vitell. 13, 1: Dom. 21 (п.).

: profusus “extravagant" is used (a) of persons, as here and Ner. 4, arrogans, profusus, immitis; (b) of things, e.g. Tit. 7, 2, convivia profusa: Vitell. 10, 2, inter profusissimos opsoniorum apparatus. Both uses are found in Cicero; e.g. Quinct. 12, perditus ac profusus nepos: Mur. 36 profusae epulae.
: = cinaedorum; see on Galb. 22.
: Dio lxvii 2, καὶ ὁ Τίτος ἰσχυρῶς περὶ τοὺς ἐκτομίας ἐσπουδάκει. Cf. Dom. 7, 1.

: Тас. Н. ii 2, Fuerunt qui (Titum) accensum desiderio Berenices reginae vertisse iter (see Tit. 5, 1) crederent. Neque abhorrebat a Berenice iuvenilis animus; sed gerendis rebus nullum ex eo impedimentum. Laetam voluptatibus adolescentiam egit, suo quam patris imperio ("reign'") moderatior: Dio lxvi 15, Βερενίκη δὲ ἰσχυρῶς τε ἤνθει, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἐς τὴν ῾Ρώμην μετὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τοῦ ᾿Αγρίππα ἦλθε. καὶ ὁ μὲν στρατηγικῶν τιμῶν ἠξιώθη, ἡ δὲ ἐν τῷ Παλατίῳ ᾤκησε, καὶ τῷ Τίτῳ συνεγίγνετο, προσεδόκα δὲ γαμηθήσεσθαι αὐτῷ, καὶ πάντα ἤδη ὡς καὶ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ οὖσα ἐποίει, ὥστ᾽ ἐκεῖνον δυσχεραίνοντας τοὺς ῾Ρωμαίους ἐπὶ τούτοις ᾐσθημένον ἀποπέμψασθαι αὐτήν; ib. c. 18, Τίτος οὐδὲν ἐρωτικὸν μοναρχήσας ἔπραξεν, ἀλλὰ σώφρων, καίτοι καὶ τῆς Βερενίκης ἐς ῾Ρώμην αὖθις ἐλθούσης, ἐγένετο. Julia Berenice was a daughter of Agrippa I, king of the Jews, and was born in 28 A.D. After a brief early marriage to Marcus, son of the alabarch Alexander, she wedded her uncle Herod, and on his death in 48 she lived (incestuously?) with her brother Agrippa II. The apostle Paul appeared before them in 60 (Acts 25, 26). She and her brother tried to dissuade the Jews from rebellion, and after the war broke out they seem to have lived in the Roman camp. She was a warm supporter of Vespasian; cf. Tac. H. ii 81, nec minore animo regina Berenice partes iuvabat, florens aetate formaque et seni quoque Vespasiano magnificentia munerum grata. In 75 she came to Rome along with her brother, and lived with Titus as though she were his wife. Juvenal (vi 157) mentions a diamond ring of hers on sale at Rome: adamans notissimus et Berenices | in digito factus pretiosior: hunc dedit olim | barbarus incestae, dedit hunc Agrippa sorori.

: Trachmann (op. cit. p. 26), commenting on the use of the indic. here, though quod . . extenderet precedes, says: Bene modum mutavit Neque enim hoc ipsum “constare” eorum, quibus rapacitas suspecta erat, sententia affertur, sed illud “solitum esse,” ita ut haec sit enuntiati conformatio: suspecta rapacitas, quod, ut constabat, solitus esset. See also on Dom. 10, 3, quod ferebatur. .. Ursinus

: restored by Torrentius for contionibus. proposed negotiationibus; Boden cocionibus; Cornelissen auctionibus. Cognitio in the special sense was a legal term for a iudicium extra ordinem, a hearing of a case not in the ordinary courts but by the emperor, the senate, or magistrates commissioned by them, such as provincial governors; cf. Claud. 15, 1, negantem cognitionis rem sed ordinarii iuris esse. In Plin. Ep. vi 31 we have examples of the variety of cognitiones conducted by Trajan aided by assessors (of whom Pliny was one), and in Ep. x 96 Pliny mentions cognitiones de Christianis by provincial governors. Cognitio was also used at times in the wider sense of iudicium, any ordinary trial (ius ordinarium).

: Titus trafficked in the influence which he could use with his father to have a case decided in a certain way. For the metaph. use of nundinari in the sense of illicit trafficking by selling or buying cf. Apul. Met. x 33, iudices sententias suas pretio nundinantur: Cic. Verr. i 119, qui ab isto ius ad utilitatem suam nundinarentur: Cic. Phil. iii 4, una in domo omnes, quorum intererat, totum imperium populi Romani nundinabantur. = praemiari: praemia pacisci (Baumg.-Cr.), "to stipulate for a reward." The word is not cited from any other author, but praemiati has been suggested as a correction of praeminate in a corrupt line of Novius (Ribb. Com. Rom. Frag. p. 257). =

: alterum, “a second"; cf. Tac. H. iv 73, ne quis alius Ariovistus regno Galliarum potiretur: Curt. ix 8, alium Liberum patrem adventare credebant: Val. Max. v 4, alius Cicero: Plin. Ep. ii 13, alius pater. This use of alius is post-class.; see Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 132: Draeger, Hist. Synt. i² 105.

: "turned out to his advantage"; cf. Sall. Iug. 22, populum Romanum neque recte neque pro bono ("to their advantage'') facturum, si etc. "Cedere pro aliqua re” meant to go for (to be counted as),'' e.g. Tac. Germ. 14, epulae . pro stipendio cedunt (see Thes. Ling. Lat. iii 732). Suetonius might have used in bonum cessit; cf. Plin. N.H. xviii 110, montium culpa in bonum cedit: Sen. Ep. 71, mala in bonum abibunt: Cic. Brut. 141, hoc vitium huic uni in bonum convertebat. .. conversa in maximas laudes: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 6, sed haec in melius conversa adeo ei immortalem gloriam contulere, ut deliciae atque amor humani generis appellaretur. •

div.p: § 2. convivia iucunda magis quam profusa: like the dinners of Augustus, Aug. 74, cenam ternis ferculis ("courses”) aut cum abundissime senis praebebat, ut non nimio sumptu, ita summa comitate.

p.note: : the term amici is not used here in the general sense of those admitted to receptions at court (salutationes, see Vesp. 4, 4); it denotes the trusted confidants and advisers (consiliarii) of Titus; cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 835, n. 3. Similarly Pliny (Pan. 88) says of the imperial freedmen of Trajan: neminem in usu habes nisi aut tibi aut patri tuo aut optimo cuique principum (especially Titus) dilectum.

: adquiescere is used by Suetonius (1) of finding peace or comfort in, Calig. 51, 3, uno solacio adquiescens; (2) of taking delight in, Tib. 56, convictores Graeculos quibus (dat.) vel maxime adquiescebat; (3) of being satisfied with, content to rely upon, as here and in Vitell. 14, 5, vaticinante Chatta muliere, cui velut oraculo adquiescebat; (4) of being content to devote one's whole attention to something, Tib. 31, negante eo destinatos magistratus abesse oportere, ut praesentes honori (i.e. their office) adquiescerent (Bentley and Mommsen would read adsuescerent). •

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 7, Denique, ut subiit pondus regium, Berenicen nuptias suas sperantem regredi domum, et enervatorum greges abire praecepit. Quo facto, quasi signum protulit mutatae intemperantiae. According to Dio (quoted above on "Berenices amorem''), Titus sent away Berenice during his father's reign, when he saw that the Roman people were displeased at the way in which she behaved as if she were already his wife; she returned to Rome when he became emperor, but he would not yield to her blandishments. The dismissal of Berenice by the emperor Titus is the theme of Racine's Bérénice, which is thus summarised by Victor Hugo: Acti Titus Act ii reginam Berenicen Act iii invitus Act iv invitam Act v dimisit. By his action Titus "freed Rome from the danger of a second Cleopatra" (von Domaszewski, Gesch. der röm. Kaiser, ii 155).
: both delicatus and delicata (Vesp. 3) were used in the sense of deliciae; cf. Petron. Satyr. 63, ipsimi nostri delicatus decessit ("my master's favourite died'').

: Suet. uses quanquam (a) c. subjunct. (never c. indic.), see on Galb. 14, 1, quanquam daret; (b) c. ptc., e.g. Galb. 19, 1, qu. haud dissimulans; (c) c. abl. abs., e.g. Vesp. 2, 2, qu. fratre adepto latum clavum; (d) c. abl. qual., e.g. Tit. 3, 1, qu. neque procera statura et ventre paulo proiectiore; (e) c. gen. qual., e.g. Ner. 20, 1, qu. exiguae vocis et fuscae; (f) c. adject., e.g. Aug. 8, 1, qu. expers belli; (g) c. subst., e.g. Claud. 35, 1, qu. iactator; (h) c. prep., Aug. 27, 5, qu. sine censurae honore. There is only one instance in Cic. of quanquam without a finite verb; Fin. v 68, si omnia illa, quae sunt extra, quanquam expetenda, summo bono continerentur (to avoid the repetition of sunt). For instances in other authors see Draeger, Hist. Synt. ii² 815; Kühner-Stegmann, ii 445. =

: for the gen. with artifex (adj. peritus) cf. Cic. Orat. 161, quod si indocta consuetudo tam est artifex suavitatis: Sall. Iug. 35, per homines talis negotii artifices: Suet. Calig. 32, 1, miles decollandi ("beheading") artifex. Bentley would read artificis, taking the adj. in a passive sense.

: cf. Euseb.-Hieron. Chron., ad a. 1974 (43 в.с.),. Publilius mimographus, natione Syrus, scaenam tenet (Teuffel-Schwabe, Röm. Lit. 212, 3). tenere scaenam means “to hold the stage, to dominate it to the exclusion of others." These delicati of Titus probably appeared on the stage as pantomimi, dancers depicting by movements and gestures (Dom. 8, 3) dramatic situations of various kinds; cf. Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 125 sqq. =
: see on Galb. 22.
: there does not seem to be any authority for taking this as amplius, diutius (“to cherish any longer," Rolfe); it must bear its ordinary meaning of liberalius (Baumg.-Cr.). ..

: Torrentius deleted coetu, and Burman regarded it as having originated from the last syllable of publico and the first of supersedit. Suetonius uses in publico for "in public" in Claud. 13, 1; 38, 2: Ner. 27, 2; 39, 3. There is no other instance of in publico coetu.

div.p: § 3. nulli civium quicquam ademit: cf. Plin. Pan. 27, nihil largiatur Princeps, dum nihil auferat.

p.note: : cf. Plin. Ep. vi 8, Atilius Crescens alieni abstinentissimus, sui diligens (contrast Sall. Cat. 5, L. Catilina alieni appetens, sui profusus): Tac. H. i 49, Galba pecuniae alienae non appetens, suae parcus, publicae avarus. So abstinentia (ἐγκράτεια χρημάτων) is opposed to avaritia and rapacitas; e.g. Dom. 9, 1:10, 1:23, 2.

: Ernesti would omit ut, but there is as unusual a pleonasm in Claud. 21, 5, immixtis interdum frigidis et arcessitis iocis: qualis est ut cum Palumbum (“The Dove," name of a gladiator) postulantibus daturum se promisit, si captus esset (Ernesti rejects qualis est as a gloss on ut). Cf. also Vesp. 7, 2, ut scilicet. In Xen. Anab. ii 6, 8 some MSS. have ἱκανός, ὡς εἴ τις καὶ ἄλλος, φροντίζειν ἦν. Plutarch and later writers use ὡς οἷον, ὡς οἷα, etc.

: in the case of some of the earlier emperors Suetonius mentions conlationes, either freely given or as involuntary as English “benevolences.” For a free-will offering cf. Aug. 57, 2, In restitutionem Palatinae domus, incendio absumptae, veterani, decuriae, tribus, atque etiam singillatim e cetero genere hominum, libenter ac pro facultate quisque contulerunt. The compulsory conlatio is illustrated by Ner. 38, 3 (after the burning of Rome), conlationibus non receptis modo verum et efflagitatis provincias privatorumque census prope exhausit: Ner. 44, 2, In praeparanda expeditione (against Vindex) partem census omnes ordines conferre iussit, et insuper inquilinos privatarum aedium; atque insularum (‘lodging-houses'") pensionem annuam repraesentare (i.e. to pay a year's rent at once) fisco. Caligula, when his daughter was born, pleaded poverty and received conlationes for the girl's maintenance and dowry (Calig. 42). On New Year's day all the citizens brought a strena or "luck-penny" to the emperor (Aug. 57, Tib. 34, Calig. 42). Pliny (Pan. 41) mentions “conlationes remisisse" among Trajan's benefactions; this presumably refers to the aurum coronarium which was paid by the provincials and others on the occasion of an emperor's accession, any great victory, or any important event in the imperial house; the payment of it was remitted by Hadrian, Alexander Severus, and Julian, as it had been by Augustus (in 29 B.C.) in the case of the Italian municipia and coloniae.
: for this form see on Vitell. 17, 1.

: the Colosseum, see Vesp. 9, 1. It was dedicated in 80 A.D. by Titus with a festival lasting 100 days. thermis: these baths of Titus were probably built, not on the ruins, but in a garden or park, of the Aurea Domus of Nero which extended from the Palatine to the Esquiline (see Oth. 7, 1). They were connected with the Flavian amphitheatre by a portico, traces of which can still be seen. It was near the site of these thermae that the famous group of Laocoon and his sons was found. The earliest thermae under the Empire were those bequeathed to Rome by M. Agrippa in the reign of Augustus. These were followed by those of Nero, Titus, Trajan, Caracalla, Diocletian, and Constantine. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 275 sqq.; Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 307 sqq. thermae, as distinct from balneae (ordinary bathing-rooms or houses), were luxurious establishments on the model of the Greek γυμνάσιον, containing, besides hot and vapour baths, all the equipment for gymnastic exercises, colonnaded halls (exedrae) where philosophers and poets congregated, etc.

: this correction by Calderinus of celebriter is based on Mart. Spect. 2, 7, Hic ubi miramur velocia munera thermas, | abstulerat miseris tecta superbus ager (i.e. Nero's proud domain had robbed the poor of their dwellings).

: munus edere (more rarely dare) was the regular phrase for giving a gladiatorial show, the giver being called editor by the writers of the Historia Augusta. So edere (dare) gladiatores (spectaculum gladiatorium). See also on munerarius in Dom. 10, 1.
: cf. Cic. Sest. 54, ludi apparatissimi et magnificentissimi.

: naumachia was used in two senses: (1) a Roman representation of a sea-fight (navale proelium); (2) as here, the place where the representation was given (= navale stagnum, Stat. S. iv 4, 5: Tac. A. xiv 15). The first public naumachia was exhibited by Julius Caesar (46 B.c.) in a district called Codeta Minor, prob. in the Campus Martius near the Tiber (Suet. Iul. 39, Dio xliii 23). The second was a representation by Augustus (2 B.C.) of the battle of Salamis in a new basin (1800 × 1200 ft., Mon. Ancyr. 23) dug in the Transtiberine region and surrounded by a grove called the nemus Caesarum after the young Lucius and Gaius (Aug. 43). The third was a splendid spectacle by Claudius (52 A.D.) on Lake Fucinus (Claud. 21: Tac. A. xii 56). Nero's naumachiae are mentioned in Dio lxi 9, lxii 15; they were held either in the amphitheatre or in the stagna Neronis, a huge basin in the grounds of Nero's Golden House. Titus exhibited two sea-fights, the one mentioned here in the vetus naumachia of Augustus, which continued in use after others had been made, and the other (between the Corcyraeans and Corinthians) in the flooded arena of the new amphitheatre (Dio lxvi 25: Mart. Spect. 24). Domitian had a new and larger lake dug below the Vatican, and also gave a naumachia in the Flavian amphitheatre (Dom. 4: Dio lxvii 8).

: in his account of the spectacles exhibited by Titus in the vetus naumachia Dio (lxvi 25) says that on the first day the basin was partly covered with planks supported on piles, and it furnished an arena for gladiatorial contests and a venatio (wild-beast hunt); on the second day, the basin being drained, there was a chariot-race; on the third, the basin being refilled, there was a naval battle of 3000 Athenians and Syracusans, in the course of which the Athenians landed on an island in the basin and took a fort there. These diverse spectacles are lauded by Martial, Spect. 28: Quidquid et in Circo spectatur et Amphitheatro, id dives, Caesar, praestitit unda tibi. | Fucinus et diri taceantur stagna Neronis: | hanc norint unam saecula naumachiam. ...

: Eutrop. vii 21, Romae amphitheatrum aedificavit, et quinque milia ferarum in dedicatione eius occidit. The total of wild and tame animals killed was 9000 according to Dio (l.c.). In the 26 venationes given by Augustus 3,500 African wild beasts were slain: Mon. Ancyr. 22, Venationes bestiarum Africanarum meo nomine aut filiorum meorum et nepotum in circo aut in foro aut in amphitheatris populo dedi sexiens et viciens, quibus confecta sunt bestiarum circiter tria milia et quingentae. At the celebration of Trajan's second Dacian triumph (107 A.D.) 11,000 animals were slain. For other examples see Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii10 81.

: cf. Dom. 4, 5, omne genus rerum missilia sparsit: Claud. 34, 2, de fabrorum ac ministrorum atque id genus numero. Originally id genus, omne genus, etc., stood in apposition to the nom. or acc., but from Varro's time are joined with other cases in a purely adverbial fashion; e.g. Varr. R.R. iii 9, 17, aliis id genus rebus: Lucr. vi 917, hoc genus in rebus. So quod genus = cuius generis; e.g. Cic. Inv. ii 157, quod genus pecunia est. Suetonius uses another adverbial acc. in Gramm. 4, 2, alia hoc genus; and in Aug. 44, 3, muliebre secus omne, Gronovius' conjecture omnes seems right. Cf. also illud aetatis in Galb. 14, 2.

: sometimes so used in post-Aug. writers referring to a point in past time "from that time on” “thenceforward,” inde ab hoc, Germ. von da an, von dem an; cf. Calig. 58, 2, duplex dehinc fama est (= de rebus quae inde ab eo tempore factae sunt, duplex est fama). See Hand 'Tursell. ii 231.

: Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 1126, shows by numerous examples that beneficia (τιμαί) was the technical term for the advantageous rights bestowed by the emperor on communities, classes, and individuals, such as the free occupation of State lands, and exemptions of various kinds. These beneficia were revocable by the emperor who granted them, and became invalid at his death. At first they were only renewed after a separate examination of each case by his successor.

: rata, which was supplied by Egnatius, gives excellent sense and would easily have been lost after aliter. Alexander proposed to omit principibus and to read beneficia a superioribus concessa <aseconcessa> aliter non haberent.

: Dio lxvi 19, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ ἄλλα πρός τε τὸ ἀσφαλές καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἄλυπον τῶν ἀνθρώπων κατεστήσατο. καὶ γὰρ γράμματα ἐξέθηκε, βεβαιῶν πάντα τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν προτέρων αὐτοκρατόρων δοθέντα τισίν, ὥστε μὴ καθ' ἑκάστους σφῶν αἰτοῦντας αὐτὸν πράγματα ἔχειν: Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 2, denique cum concessa per priores principes firmari ab insequentibus mos esset, simul imperium cepit, talia possidentibus edicto sponte cavit. The edicts of the emperors were a continuation of the magisterial edicts of Republican times. Sometimes they contained a definite command, sometimes a mere communication or exhortation or remonstrance (cf. Mommsen, ii 905; Hardy on Plin. Ep. x 58). Augustus used them even to answer lampoons: iocis quorundam invidiosis aut petulantibus lacessitus, contradixit edicto (Aug. 56, 1, where see Shuckburgh). Claudius issued as many as 20 in a day, one being "ut uberi vinearum proventu bene dolia picarentur, (Claud. 16, 4). The innovation of Titus in confirming previous beneficia by one general edict was followed by subsequent emperors. Pliny (Ep. x 58) has recorded in full the edict of Nerva; Domitian's is mentioned by Dio (lxvii 2), and that of Marcus Aurelius by his son Commodus (quoted in Dig. xxvii 1, 8). .. :

: Bentley ingeniously suggested that this is a corruption of hunc morem; cf. Ner. 15, 1, cognoscendi morem eum tenuit, ut Galb. 4, 4, morem obstinatissime retinuit, ut On the other hand, homines is often used by Suetonius for the people" "the emperor's subjects"; e.g. Ner. 39, 1, mirum fuerit nihil eum patientius quam maledicta et convicia hominum tulisse. Bentley would further alter tenuit ne to tenuit ut ne, which is quite needless.

: "held firmly to his rule of not..." Livy and later writers use tenere with ut or ne in the sense of carrying one's point; e.g. Liv. ii 42, 2, tenuere patres, ut Fabius consul crearetur: iv 30, 16, plebs tenuit, ne consules in proximum annum crearentur: Plin. Ep. vi 5, scripseram tenuisse Varenum ut sibi evocare testes liceret.
: cf. Vesp. 22, admonente dispensatore.
: for quasi see on c. 5, 3.

: Eutrop. vii 21, facilitatis et liberalitatis tantum fuit, ut, cum nulli quicquam negaret et ab amicis reprehenderetur, responderit nullum tristem debere ab imperatore discedere: Cedrenus (p. 178), ἀπὸ βασιλέως δεῖ σκυθρωπὸν μὴ ἀποπέμπεσθαι. For tristis used of a disappointed applicant cf. Lucr. iii 997, Qui petere a populo fasces saevasque secures | imbibit et semper victus tristisque recedit.

: "over" i.e. "during" dinner. Cf. Germ. über Tische, über Tafel; Gr. ἐπὶ δείπνῳ, ἐπὶ κύλικι (Baumg.-Cr.). super in a temporal sense (= inter) is post-Aug. and found only in a few phrases: super cenam (11 times in Suet., e.g. Vesp. 22: Vitell. 12: Dom. 14, 1:21; Curt. viii 43: Plin. Ep. iii 5, etc.: Juv. xv 14); super mensam (Curt. vii 4); super mensas et pocula (Flor. iv 2, 69); super vinum et epulas (Curt. viii 4); super hos divum .. honores (Stat. Th. i 676). recordatus = =

: the use of quod instead of the acc. and inf. is fully discussed by Madvig (Opusc. Acad. ii 232 sqq.) and Kühner-Stegmann (ii 274 sqq.). There are a few apparent instances in old Lat.: Plaut. Asin. 52, scio iam filius quod amet meus istanc meretricem (where Brix takes quod amet as amicam): Cato in Plin. N.H. 29, 14, quod bonum sit illorum litteras inspicere, non perdiscere, vincam (where some explain quod bonum sit as quid boni sit). In class. Lat. there is no sure instance. The first certain example is in Auct. Bell. Hisp. 36, renuntiarunt quod Pompeium in potestate haberent. In post-class. times it occurs in Petron. 71, scis, quod epulum dedi: Plin. Ep. ii 11, 6, adnotatum experimentis, quod ... habent: Justin i 7, 9, cognito quod inlatum Croeso bellum esset: Tac. A. xiv 6, reputans ideo se fallacibus litteris accitam et praecipuo honore habitam, quodque litus iuxta non ventis acta navis concidisset (where quodque may be taken as et id, quod). From the middle of the 2nd cent. it occurs with increasing frequency in Apuleius, Gellius, the Scriptores Hist. Aug., Eutropius, Ammianus, and the = Christian writers. The use in Gr. of οἵνεκα, ὁθούνεκα, διότι instead of ὅτι with verba sentiendi and declarandi is similar.

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 9, Quadam etiam die, recordans vesperi nihil se cuiquam praestitisse, venerando caelestique dicto "Amici,” ait, “perdidimus diem”: quia erat magnificae liberalitatis: Themistius Orat. vi, Τίτου τοῦ γενναίου τὸ λαμπρὸν καὶ μέγα ἐκεῖνο ῥῆμα, ὅτι Τήμερον οὐκ ἐβασίλευσα· οὐδὲν γὰρ εὖ ἐποίησα: Zonaras xi 18, Τούτου ἐστὶ καὶ ἡ ἀοίδιμος ἐκείνη φωνή, εἰπόντος: σήμερον οὐκ ἐβασίλευσα, ἐπεὶ οὐδένα εὐηργέτησα. Ausonius, Grat. Act. xvi, says that the fame of the utterance was due to the contrast of such generosity with the meanness of Vespasian: Celebre fuit Titi Caesaris dictum, perdidisse se diem, quo nihil boni fecerat; sed celebre fuit, quia Vespasiani successor dixerat, cuius nimia parsimonia et austeritas vix ferenda miram fecerat filii lenitatem.

: since Eutropius (vii 21, 3) gives the utterance as “amici, hodie diem perdidi" (so too Euseb.-Hieron. Chron.) and Themistius and Zonaras have τήμερον and σήμερον, Casaubon would read hodie diem here. Hase quotes from the speech of Titus in Racine's Bérénice (iv 4): “Où sont ces heureux jours que je faisais attendre? | Quels pleurs ai-je séchés?
