Dans quels yeux satisfaits | Ai-je déjà goûté le fruit de mes bienfaits? | L'univers a-t-il vu changer ses destinées? | Sais-je combien le ciel m'a compté de journées? | Et de ce peu de jours, si longtemps attendus, | Ah! malheureux! combien j'en ai déjà perdus!” Pliny (Pan. 56) in his flattery of Trajan says that he did not let even a moment pass without some benefaction: Quod momentum, quod immo temporis punctum, aut beneficio sterile, aut vacuum laude? So too Ausonius (l.c.) says to Gratianus: "Neque vero unum aliquod bonum uno die praestas, sed indulgentias saeculares per singula horarum momenta multiplicas.”

div.p: § 2. proposito: sc. per edictum; cf. Aug. 42, 2, proposito congiario: Ner. 7, 2, populo congiarium, militi donativum proposuit: Claud. 18, 2, negotiatoribus certa lucra proposuit.

p.note: : see on c. 7, 3.

: Pliny (Pan. 33) says the same of Trajan's readiness to give spectacles: Impetratum est quod postulabatur; oblatum quod non postulabatur; institit ultro, et, ut concupisceremus, admonuit. The adv. ultro meant (1) ‘to the further side" (opp. to citro); (2) "furthermore”; (3) ‘beyond what could be expected of one,” “of one's own accord." Gladiators who were kept in reserve and only produced at the special request of the spectators were called postulaticii (Sen. Ερ. 7, 4).

: the class of gladiators known as Thraeces were so called from their small round shields like those of the Thracians (a similitudine parmularum Thraciarum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 366 M.); cf. parmae Threcidicae, Plin. N.H. xxxiii 129. They carried a short curved sword (sica, Suet. Calig. 32; falx supina, Juv. viii 201) and wore greaves (ocreae). They were usually pitted against murmillones (so called from the image of a fish mormyr, μορμύρος, on their helmets), who were heavily armed and carried a big oblong shield (scutum). Caligula fought as a Thraex, and reduced the amount of armour of the murmillones (Suet. Calig. 54, 55). On one occasion a murmillo fought him in a sham contest with wooden swords (rudes) and fell on purpose, whereupon Caligula stabbed him with a real sica, and ran about with a palm-branch as victors do (ib. 32). The form Thraex, to denote a gladiator, is attested by the best MSS. and by inscriptions (see Orelli-Mewes on Hor. S. ii 6, 44, Thraex est Gallina Syro par?); Thrax meant a Thracian. =

: this is rightly explained by Baumg.-Cr. as cum populo, diversae factioni favente, iocose altercatus est ut fautor Thraecum. Suetonius always uses cavillatio in the sense of a jest or witticism; cf. Vesp. 23, 1, ut invidiam aliqua cavillatione dilueret: Tib. 57, 2, acerba cavillatio “a brutal witticism": Gramm. 3, cavillatio nominis "a pun on a name." For cavillari cum cf. Cic. Att. ii 1, 5, familiariter cum ipso cavillor ac iocor.

: partizanship in the amphitheatre, though not so intense as in the circus, was very strong among all classes, and some of the emperors were notorious for it. This partizanship was exhibited not only towards individual gladiators, but also towards the various kinds of combatants (Friedl. Sitteng. ii10 75). Caligula and Titus favoured the Thraeces; Domitian the murmillones (see Dom. 10, 1, and notes there). Tacitus (H. ii 91) says of Vitellius: omnem infimae plebis rumorem ("applause") in theatro ut spectator, in circo ut fautor adfectavit.

: cf. Tac. A. i 47, maiestate salva, cui maior e longinquo reverentia. Contrast the undignified conduct of Claudius at the gladiatoria munera, as described in Claud. 21, 5: Nec ullo spectaculi genere communior aut remissior erat, adeo ut oblatos victoribus aureos ("gold coins") prolata sinistra pariter cum vulgo voce digitisque numeraret ac saepe hortando rogandoque ad hilaritatem homines provocaret, "dominos" identidem appellans, immixtis interdum frigidis et arcessitis (“farfetched'') iocis. Vespasian too was lacking in dignity in his lighter moments; see Vesp. 22.

: the same impartiality in observing the leges harenae and bestowing on the victors the promised rewards, regardless of the class to which they belonged, is attributed to Trajan by Pliny, Pan. 33, Quam deinde in edendo (munere gladiatorio) liberalitatem, quam iustitiam exhibuit omni affectione aut intactus aut maior!
: cf. Vesp. 8, 3, ne quam occasionem corrigendi disciplinam praetermitteret.
: see c. 7, 3.

: an example followed by Alexander Severus; cf. Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 42, Thermis et suis et veterum frequenter cum populo usus est, et aestate maxime, balneari veste ad Palatium revertens, hoc solum imperatorium habens quod lacernam cocceam accipiebat. Einhard (c. 22) relates the same of Charlemagne: Non solum filios ad balneum, verum optimates et amicos, aliquando etiam satellitum et custodum corporis turbam invitavit; ita ut nonnunquam centum vel eo amplius homines lavarentur.

div.p: § 3. sub eo: "in his reign"; cf. Calig. 21, opera sub Tiberio semiperfecta: Tac. Agr. 6, gnarus sub Nerone temporum: ib. 45, praecipua sub Domitiano miseriarum pars erat. Such designations of time are post-class. (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 557).

p.note: : the subst. fortuita (= fortuito accidentia) is used of accidents of fortune, disasters; cf. Ner. 39, 1, Accesserunt tantis ex principe malis probrisque quaedam et fortuita: pestilentia unius autumni, etc.; Tac. A. xiv 3, nihil tam capax fortuitorum quam mare. =
: intensive, ac quidem. Kühner-Stegmann, ii 16.

: the famous eruption on the 24th of August, 79 A.D., which overwhelmed Herculaneum and Pompeii. It is vividly described by Pliny in two letters to Tacitus (vi 16 and 20); his uncle, the elder Pliny, perished in it. See also Dio lxvi 21-23. The earthquake which accompanied it caused widespread havoc in Campania. The corruptions in the MSS. make it impossible to determine which of the various forms of the name of the volcano (Vesuvius, Vesevus, Vesaevus, Vesvius, Vesbius) was used by Suetonius. Here ue*bii is the reading of M, uesubii of G, ueseui of N; a few lines later M has uesuuio, G uesubio, L uesieuio, the rest ueseuio or ueseuo. Roth and Preud'homme adopt the form Vesvius, Ihm Vesuvius.

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 12, Huius tempore mons Vesuvius in Campania ardere coepit, incendiumque Romae sine nocturna requie per triduum fuit. Dio (lxvi 24) mentions that the fire occurred in 80 A.D., while Titus was absent from Rome relieving the distress in Campania; he also gives a list of the principal buildings which were destroyed by the fire: πῦρ δὲ δὴ ἕτερον ἐπίγειον τῷ ἑξῆς ἔτει πολλὰ πάνυ τῆς Ῥώμης, τοῦ Τίτου πρὸς τὸ πάθημα τὸ ἐν τῇ Καμπανίᾳ γενόμενον ἐκδημήσαντος, ἐπενείματο. καὶ γὰρ τὸ Σεραπεῖον, καὶ τὸ Ἰσεῖον, τά τε Σεπτά, καὶ τὸ Ποσειδώνιον, τό τε βαλανεῖον τὸ τοῦ ᾿Αγρίππου, καὶ τὸ Πάνθειον, τό τε Διριβιτώριον, καὶ τὸ τοῦ Βάλβου θέατρον, καὶ τὴν τοῦ Πομπηίου σκηνήν, καὶ τὰ Ὀκταουίεια οἰκήματα μετὰ τῶν βιβλίων, τόν τε νεὼν τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ Καπιτωλίου μετὰ τῶν συννάων αὐτοῦ κατέκαυσεν. Of these buildings the Serapeum, Isaeum, Saepta, Templum Neptuni, Thermae Agrippae, Pantheon, Diribitorium, Theatrum Balbi, Scaena (Theatrum) Pompeii, and Porticus Octaviae (with the library) were all situated in the southern part of the Campus Martius, on the north side of the Capitoline.

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 13, lues quoque, quanta vix unquam antea fuit. This must be the plague at Rome in which on many days about 10,000 perished, assigned to the reign of Vespasian in Euseb.-Hieron. Chron. (ad a. 2093, i.e. 77 A.D.): Lues ingens Romae facta, ita ut per multos dies in ephemeridem decem milia ferme mortuorum referrentur. Dio (lxvi 23) says that the ashes from Vesuvius were carried to Rome (also to Africa, Egypt, and Syria) and overhung the city, obscuring the sun, and that this was the cause of the pestilence which came later: ἡ μὲν οὖν τέφρα αὕτη οὐδὲν μέγα τότε κακὸν αὐτοὺς εἰργάσατο, ὕστερον δὲ νόσον σφίσι λοιμώδη δεινὴν ἐνέβαλε. Plagues raged at Rome and throughout Italy in 23 and 22 B.C. (Dio liii 33, liv 1), and in 65 A.D. during Nero's reign Rome was devastated by a pestilence, the horrors of which are depicted in Tac. A. xvi 13; the 30,000 burials recorded in the Temple of Libitina during that autumn were only a fractional part of the total mortality (Friedlaender, Sitteng. i¹º 31).
: see on c. 6, 2.
: Cornelissen suggested fatalibus.

: this use of sed et for sed etiam is post-class. (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 59). Suetonius also uses non modo sed etiam; non modo verum et; non solum verum et (or etiam); non tantum sed et (or etiam); non solum sed et (or etiam).
: affectus (subst.) in the sense of amor or benevolentia is post-class. In class. Lat. it denotes any state or disposition of mind (or body). See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 116.

: Hadrian acted in a similar way in the face of like calamities; Spart. Hadr. 21, Fuerunt eius temporibus fames, pestilentia, terrae motus, quae omnia, quantum potuit, procuravit multisque civitatibus vastatis per ista subvenit.

div.p: § 4. curatores restituendae Campaniae: Dio lxvi 24, ὁ δ᾽ οὖν Τίτος τοῖς μὲν Καμπανοῖς δύο ἄνδρας ἐκ τῶν ὑπατευκότων (consularium) οἰκιστὰς ἔπεμψε, καὶ χρήματα ἄλλα τε καὶ τὰ τῶν ἄνευ κληρονόμων τεθνηκότων ἐδωρήσατο· αὐτὸς δὲ οὐδὲν οὔτε παρ᾿ ἰδιώτου, οὔτε παρὰ πόλεως, οὔτε παρὰ βασιλέως, καίτοι πολλῶν πολλὰ διδόντων αὐτῷ καὶ ὑπισχνουμένων, ἔλαβεν· ἀνέστησε μέντοι καὶ ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων πάντα. The appointment of these ex-consuls as οἰκισταί, or founders of new settlements, was a concession on the part of Titus to the senate; see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 996 n. Titus' restorations are mentioned in an inscription (in both Gr. and Lat.) at Naples in Campania, date July, 80-June, 81, C.I.L. x 1481, Newton 101: [Αὐτοκράτωρ] Τίτος Καίσαρ θεοῦ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ υἱὸς Ο]ὐεσπασιανὸς Σεβαστός, [ἀρχιερεὺς μέγιστος, δημαρχ]ικῆς ἐξουσίας τὸ ί, [αὐτοκράτωρ τὸ ιέ, πατὴρ πατρίδος, ὕπατος τὸ ή, τειμητής, [ἐν Νέᾳ πόλει δημαρχήσας, ἀγων]ο θετήσας τὸ γ' γυμνασιαρχήσας [ὑπὸ σεισμῶν συμπεσόντα ἀποκατέστησεν. [Imp. Titus Caesar divi Vespasia]ni f. Vespasianus Aug., [pont. max., trib. pot. x, imp. xv,] cos. viii, censor, p.p., [terrae mo]tibus conlapsa restituit. For Vespasian's restoration of a temple at Herculaneum which had been wrecked by an earlier earthquake in 62 A.D. see on Vesp. 17.

p.note: : these, as bona vacantia, would escheat to the fiscus.

: there is considerable variation in the MSS. here: nichil nisi sibi perisse testatus publice (r); nichil nisi sibi publice perisse testatus (OT vulg.); nichil nisi sibi perisse publice testatus (N); nihil publice perisse testatus (Torrentius, from what he describes as an "optimus codex," now unknown; Roth and Preud 'homme adopt this reading). The confusion seems due to a mistaken effort to connect the words nihil publice with perisse and not with testatus; but the latter is the right construction, as is shown by Oth. 6, 3: nihil magis pro contione testatus est, quam id demum se habiturum, quod sibi illi reliquissent. Possibly se should be inserted after nisi. The only public pronouncement of Titus was that he was a ruined man, i.e. that he would be ruined by the cost of the rebuilding which he had at once resolved to undertake at his own expense. Alexander (op. cit. p. 20) thinks the original reading was nihil publice nisi sibi perisse testatus which he translates "nothing had perished in a public way save only so far as he was concerned," the meaning being that Titus would shoulder the whole burden and that there would be no extra tax-levies on the unfortunate citizens to restore the ruined edifices. But though either nihil publice perisse or nihil nisi sibi perisse would be intelligible, nihil publice nisi sibi perisse seems very improbable.

: praetorium was used in the sense of a country mansion; see Mayor on Juv. i 75 (criminibus debent hortos praetoria mensas) where he cites Colum. i 6 to show that the villa in the wider sense, country seat, was divided into (1) urbana, hall or residence; (2) rustica, farm; (3) fructuaria, stores, barns, etc.; and the urbana as "the headquarters of the peaceful camp" was named praetorium (Pallad. i 8, 2 etc.). Augustus disliked palatial country mansions (Aug. 72, 2, ampla et operosa praetoria gravabatur). Caligula in building praetoria delighted in overcoming natural obstacles by filling up seas and valleys and cutting away rocks and mountains (Calig. 37, 2). praetorium has the same sense in Tib. 39; Stat. S. i 3, 25: Mart. x 79, etc. Suetonius also uses it for the headquarters in a camp (e.g. Vitell. 8, 2) and for the praetorian guard (e.g. Tit. 6, 1).

: for the dative of purpose see on Oth. 3, 1. The acc. with mederi (instead of the usual dat.) is very rare; it occurs once in Terence (Phorm. 822) and then not till Livy (see the instances collected by Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre iii 5).

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 14, quibus tamen malis, nullo vexato, pecunia propria subvenit, cunctis remediorum generibus, nunc aegrotantes per semetipsum reficiens, nunc consolans suorum mortibus afflictos.
: the plague was interpreted as a manifestation of divine wrath for some offence which required to be expiated by the sacrifice of hostiae piaculares.

div.p: §5. adversa: subst. = mala, calamitates; so a few lines earlier, in iis tot adversis ac talibus.

p.note: : this term for “informers” was derived from the giving in the name (delatio nominis) of an accused person to the presidents of the quaestiones perpetuae. The rewards to be obtained in some cases, even under the Republic, from the goods of the condemned led to the quadruplatores (later delatores) becoming a professional class. Under the early Empire Tacitus describes delatores as “genus hominum publico exitio repertum et ne poenis quidem satis coercitum’” (Ann. iv 30). Among their many activities they denounced to the agents of the imperial Treasury any possession of property which the Treasury could claim (res fisci). They profited by the praemia given by Augustus for convictions of violations of his marriage laws, and especially by the Lex Iulia de maiestate (lèse-majesté) which gave the accuser + of the estate of the condemned. Tiberius at first discouraged, but afterwards encouraged them (Tib. 61: Tac. A. i 73, iv 30). Caligula on his accession “negavit se delatoribus aures habere" (Calig. 15, 4), and Nero in his early days reduced their rewards (Ner. 10, 1). Domitian began by repressing them (Dom. 9, 3), but later used them as tools for his extortions (Dom. 12, 1). Trajan followed the example of Titus by punishing them severely and banishing them (Plin. Pan. 34, 44). mandatores: those who suborn, or furnish materials to, informers (delatores). The jurist Callistratus (Dig. xlix 14, 2) says that under the Antonines mandatores were to be punished equally with delatores: Divus Pius Caecilio Maximo rescripsit constitutionem patris sui, qua compelleretur delator edere mandatorem ac, nisi edidisset, ut in vincula deduceretur, eo pertinere, non ut delator poenae subduceretur, si mandatorem haberet, sed ut mandator quoque perinde atque si ipse detulisset puniretur: cf. xlix 14, 24, non tantum delator punitur, si non probaverit, sed et mandator: quem exhibere debet delator. There can be no doubt that mandatores is the right reading in our passage, but Ihm keeps amendatores, the reading of M.

: cf. Mart. vi 46, vapulat assidue veneti quadriga flagello: Pelagon. 365, assidue aut flagello aut voce excitari debet: Salvian. de gub. dei i 57, assidue flagellamur: Suet. Calig. 30, 2, equestrem ordinem assidue proscidit ('tongue-lashed," Rolfe). ..

: cf. Lamprid. Comm. 18, where the outcries of the senate against the delatores at the death of Commodus are quoted: “Nunc securi sumus; delatoribus metum. Ut securi simus, delatoribus metum. Ut salvi simus, delatores de senatu, delatoribus fustem. Te salvo delatores ad leonem. Te imperante delatoribus fustem.” "Now at last we are secure; let informers tremble. That we may be secure, let informers tremble. That we may be safe, cast informers out of the senate, the club for informers! While you are safe, to the lions with informers! While you are ruler, the club for informers!" (Magie). Marcilius points out that slaves were beaten with flagella, free men with fustes; cf. Macer (Dig. xlviii 19, 10): Ex quibus causis liber fustibus caeditur, ex his servus flagellis caedi, et domino reddi iubetur; et ex quibus liber fustibus caesus in opus publicum damnatur, ex his servus sub poena vinculorum, ad eius temporis spatium, flagellis caesus domino reddi iubetur. The delatores, as free men about to be sold as slaves, receive both punishments.

: Martial (Spect. 4) refers to this: Turba gravis paci placidaeque inimica quieti, | quae semper miseras sollicitabat opes, | traducta est, ingens nec cepit harena nocentes: | et delator habet quod dabat exilium. | Exulat Ausonia profugus delator ab urbe: | haec licet impensis principis adnumeres. Friedlaender (on Mart. l.c.) suggests that this exhibition of the delatores took place in the early morning, like the executions in the amphitheatre before the regular spectacles. traducere means 'to lead in procession as in a triumph"; e.g. Liv. xxxvi 40, cum captivis nobilibus equorum quoque captorum gregem traduxit.

: sc. hastae or praeconi (sub praeconem and voci praeconis subicere are also used by Cic.); cf. Aug. 24, 1, ipsum bonaque subiecit hastae. For subicere used absolutely cf. Calig. 38, 4, reliquias omnium spectaculorum subiecit et venditavit.

: Pliny (Pan. 35) mentions the edictum Titi against the delatores, and says that Nerva made some additions to it, while Trajan improved it so much that he might be regarded as the originator of it. Suetonius uses imperare 16 times with the acc. and inf. pass. (in Tib. 57, 2 with the inf. act. and pass., adtractum ad se recipere debitum ducique ad supplicium imperavit); once with ut (Calig. 46), and once with the subjunct. without ut (Ner. 1, 1).

: cf. Sen. ad Helv. 6, 4, deserta loca et asperrimas insulas Sciathum et Seriphum, Gyarum et Corsicam percense: nullum invenies exilium, in quo non aliquis animi causa moretur. For insularum instead of insulas cf. Liv. x 2, gravissimas navium; xxviii 39, terrarum ultimas. Banishment to islands was common under the Empire; e.g. Augustus banished his daughter Julia to Pandataria, off Latium, and later her son Agrippa to Planasia, off Etruria (Aug. 19:65); Tiberius banished his daughter-in-law to Pandataria (Tib. 53), and the son of Germanicus to Pontia, off Latium. The different grades of banishment distinguished by Callistratus (Dig. xlviii 19, 28) are (1) in insulam deportatio, (2) deportatio, (3) in insulam relegatio, (4) in perpetuum relegatio, (5) in tempus relegatio. (deportatio involved loss of all civil and personal rights, relegatio loss of none; Vesp. 15, n.) The miseries of an exile on a barren isle are illustrated by Seneca's epigrams on his exile in Corsica. An exhaustive account of such banishment will be found in Mayor's note on Juv. i 73, aude aliquid brevibus Gyaris (islet in Aegaean) et carcere dignum, | si vis esse aliquid.

: cf. Iul. 66, vetustissima nave impositos quocumque vento in quascumque terras iubebo avehi: Ter. Phorm. 977, non hoc publicitus scelus hinc asportarier | in solas terras! Dio (lxvi 19) merely says that Titus banished the delatores from Rome: τοὺς μηνυτὰς ἐξήλασεν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως.

p.mentioned: vetuit de eadem re pluribus legibus agi
p.note: : to prevent the delatores, in the event of their having unsuccessfully brought a charge under a certain law, from renewing the charge under some other law. This enactment of Titus was in accordance with the general principle of Roman civil law that a matter once tried should not be tried again (except by way of appeal), even though the form of suit was different. Fresh proceedings were (with certain exceptions) barred by the Exceptio rei iudicatae; cf. Ulp. Dig. xliv 2, 7, 4, Exceptio obstat quotiens inter easdem personas eadem quaestio revocatur vel alio genere iudicii; xliv 2, 5, De eadem re agere videtur et qui non eadem actione agat, qua ab initio agebat, sed etiam si alia experiatur, de eadem tamen re. (Roby, Rom. Priv. Law ii 388 sqq.)

: the legal position of a person according as he was freeborn (ingenuus), freedman (libertus), or slave (servus). The delatores would try to prove that a deceased person had had no right to the status of free-born, and that so his testamentary dispositions were invalid.

: the number of years is unknown; it may have been five, the number fixed later by Nerva and Marcus Aurelius; cf. Callistr. Dig. xl 15, 4, primus omnium divus Nerva edicto vetuit, post quinquennium mortis cuiusque de statu quaeri (the words primus omnium contradict what Suet. says about Titus); Capitol., Marc. Anton. 10, de statu etiam defunctorum intra quinquennium quaeri iussit. Marcus Aurelius also ordained that if any one had been formally declared freeborn (ingenuus), no revision of this declaration could be made except during his lifetime, and that any suit commenced for contesting such a declaration was at once extinguished by his death. Hadrian decided that the status of a living person could not be questioned if it would affect that of a person dead more than five years; cf. Dig. xl 15, 1, where Marcianus states that at times the five years' limitation was not observed if the investigation was in favour of, and not prejudicial to, the deceased, e.g. to show that the mother of a living slave was a freewoman and not an ancilla. See Roby, op. cit. i 50. 2 к

: the chief pontificate, the highest religious power, was conferred apart from the other imperial powers on all the emperors from Augustus to Gratianus, who (c. 382) formally renounced it, and none of his successors appears as pontiff. It usually comes first in the order of imperial titles recorded in inscriptions; e.g. C.I.L. ii 4838, Imp. Tito Caesare Vespasiano Aug., pont. max., trib. pot. IX, imp. XV, p. p., cos. VIII. It had been conferred on Julius Caesar, and on his assassination it was usurped by Lepidus, on whose death (13 в.с.), and not before, Augustus accepted it (Aug. 31, 1). As pontifex maximus the emperor could deal with all offences against religion. It was in this capacity that Domitian punished the Vestal virgins charged with incest (Dom. 8, 3). The office also carried great powers of patronage, and the emperor by his nomination or commendation could secure admission for his favourites to the religious colleges. See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 72, 780, 783, 1106 sqq.; Greenidge, Rom. Public Life p. 351.

: as the context shows, puras here means free from bloodguiltiness, a limited meaning which occurs e.g. in Hor. S. i 4, 68, at bene si quis | et vivat puris manibus (where see Palmer); so καθαραὶ (opp. to φονίαι) χεῖρες, Aesch. Eum. 313, etc. Bremi refers to the belief that it was a pollution for a priest even to look upon a corpse.

: Dio lxvi 19, οὐ μὴν ἀλλ᾽ ὁ Τίτος οὐδένα τῶν βουλευτῶν (senatorum) ἐν τῇ αὑτοῦ ἡγεμονίᾳ ἀπέκτεινεν, ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ ἄλλος τις αὐτῷ ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτοῦ ἀρχῆς ἐτελεύτησεν: C. 18, ὁ δὲ δὴ Τίτος οὐδὲν φονικὸν . . μοναρχήσας ἔπραξεν, ἀλλὰ χρηστός, καίπερ ἐπιβουλευθείς, ἐγένετο. Ausonius (Caes. xi) praises Titus as "expers civilis sanguinis, orbis amor." Cf. also Oros. vii 9, 13, cuius tanta tranquillitas in imperio fuit, ut nullius omnino sanguinem in re publica administranda fudisse referatur: Eutrop. vii 21, 2, Romae tantae civilitatis in imperio fuit, ut nullum omnino puniret, convictos adversum se coniurationis dimiserit, et in eadem qua antea familiaritate habuerit. Nerva took an oath in the senate that he would not slay any senator, and he kept his pledge in spite of plots against him (Dio lxviii 2). duos patricii generis, etc.: Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 3, Neque minus sancte facilis in tuendis, qui forte in se coniuravissent, adeo ut, cum amplissimi ordinis duo abnuere cogitatum scelus nequirent patresque censuissent de confessis supplicium sumendum, deductos in spectaculum se utrimque adsidere iusserit petitoque ex industria gladiatoris (mirmillonum, Epit. 10, 3), quorum pugnae visebantur, gladio quasi ad explorandam aciem uni atque alteri committeret. Queis perculsis et constantiam mirantibus: "videtisne,” inquit, “potestates fato dari frustraque temptari facinus potiundi spe vel amittendi metu?” Dio (lxviii 3) tells precisely the same story about Nerva, except that the emperor's daring is made the more remarkable by the statement that the conspirators, when invited to the gladiatorial show, had no knowledge that their plot had been detected. Aelian (Var. Hist. vi 14) describes how Dareius, son of Hystaspes, dealt in the same bold fashion with Aribazus, when he conspired with others to slay the Persian king during a hunt.

: for this constr. cf. Claud. 14, in maiore fraude convictos: Cic. Sull. 83, in hoc scelere convictus. Suetonius also uses (a) the gen., Tib. 1, 2, alter latrocinii, caedis alter convictus est; (b) the abl., Ner. 31, 3, scelere convictos; (c) the inf., Vesp. 4, 3, convictus ducenta sestertia expressisse iuveni.

: though adfectare in the sense of niti ad, cum studio expetere occurs from Sallust on, the subst. adfectatio is not found before Val. Max. In other passages of Suet. it is used for literary affectation; Tib. 70, 1, adfectatione et morositate nimia obscurabat stilum; Gramm. 10, 1, nimia priscorum verborum adfectatione.

: Julius Caesar had acted in the same lenient way towards conspirators; cf. Iul. 75, 4, Si qua posthac aut cogitarentur gravius adversus se aut dicerentur, inhibere maluit quam vindicare. Itaque et detectas coniurationes conventusque nocturnos non ultra arguit, quam ut edicto ostenderet esse sibi notas, et acerbe loquentibus satis habuit pro contione denuntiare ne perseverarent. For the elliptical nihil amplius quam see on Dom. 21, nihil aliud quam deambulabat. •

div.p: § 2. cursores suos: Domitian's couriers are mentioned in Tac. Agr. 43, supremo quidem die momenta ipsa deficientis (Agricolae) per dispositos cursores nuntiata constabat.`

p.note: : see on c. 8, 3. ..

: a special mark of imperial favour; cf. Ner. 22, 3, Instituerant civitates, apud quas musici agones edi solent, omnes citharoedorum coronas ad ipsum (Neronem) mittere. Eas adeo grate recipiebat, ut legatos, qui pertulissent, non modo primos admitteret, sed etiam familiaribus epulis interponeret.
: see on c. 4, 3; cf. Liv. xlii 52, 5, constitit in tribunali circa se habens filios duos.
: "deliberately," Gr. ἐπιτηδές; cf. Vesp. 16, 2: Dom. 16, 2:19. Suetonius also uses the Ciceronian de industria, e.g. Galb. 19, 2. Livy seems to be the first to use ex.

: ferramenta, which usually means iron tools, is very rarely used as here in the sense of arma; cf. Cic. Sull. 19, in munere servili obtulit se ad ferramenta prospicienda; id. Cat. iii 5. At the gladiatorial spectacles, after the opening parade of the gladiators through the arena, there was often some sham fighting with harmless weapons (arma lusoria) in which gladiators gave a display of their exercises and noble amateurs often took part; Dio (lxvi 15) says that Titus defeated Alienus (prob. the consul in 69) in such sham fighting at games in his native place Reate. When this terminated, the giver of the spectacle (editor) was asked to examine the real weapons (arma pugnatoria, decretoria) about to be used, to see that they conformed with the regulations. Drusus, son of Tiberius, apparently conducted this probatio armorum with rigour, and the variety of gladiator's sword with the sharpest edge was called after him (Δρουσιανὰ ξίφη, Dio lvii 13). Domitian at his spectacles seems to have deprived the gladiators of defensive armour (see Friedl. on Mart. viii 80). Marcus Aurelius, when he presided at the shows given in his name, would only allow the combatants to use blunted swords (gladii 2 к 2 hebetes) or weapons with the point protected by a ball or button (arma praepilata). See Friedl., Sitteng. ii¹º 73; Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1594.

: genitura meant (a) the day and hour of birth, (b) the calculations based upon this by the soothsayers or astrologers (genethliaci, mathematici, astrologi, Chaldaei, Babylonii) who cast the horoscopes or nativities predicting the future fate or fortune of the child from the position of the stars at its birth; cf. Vitell. 3, 2, Vesp. 25. The Greek word γένεσις was also used in Lat. for a horoscope; e.g. Vesp. 14: Dom. 10, 3: Juv. xiv 248, nota mathematicis genesis tua. Suetonius (Aug. 94, 12) tells how Augustus and Agrippa visited a mathematicus, Theogenes, in Apollonia, who predicted great good fortune for Agrippa. Augustus at first, fearing a less favourable forecast, would not divulge the time of his birth (reticere genituram suam perseverabat). At last the mathematicus prevailed on him to do so, and when he heard it, Theogenes sprang up and paid homage. Augustus afterwards had such confidence in his destiny that he published the thema or horoscope, and struck a silver coin with Capricorn, his natal star, upon it. Later emperors were experts in astrology; e.g. Tiberius (who foretold the rise of Galba, Galb. 4, 1, n.), Hadrian, and Septimius Severus (Spartian. Sever. 2, in quadam civitate Africana, cum sollicitus mathematicum consuluisset positaque hora ingentia vidisset astrologus, dixit ei “tuam, non alienam, pone genituram’'; cumque Severus iurasset suam esse, omnia ei dixit quae postea facta sunt: c. 3, cum amissa uxore aliam vellet ducere, genituras sponsarum requirebat, ipse quoque matheseos peritissimus, et cum audisset esse in Syria quandam quae id geniturae haberet ut regi iungeretur, eandem uxorem petit).

: "at some future time," the prevalent meaning of the word in Suetonius; but he also has it in its other sense of "whenever" (= quandocumque), e.g. Claud. 1, 4, se rei p. statum, quandoque posset, restituturum.

div.p: § 3. fratrem insidiari sibi non desinentem: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 11, fratrem quoque Domitianum parantem insidias, militumque animos sollicitantem flens saepius obtestatus est, ne parricidio assequi cuperet, quod et se volente esset obventurum ei et iam haberet, cum sit particeps potestatis. The plotting of Domitian against Titus from the time of Vespasian's death is described in Dom. 2, 3, neque cessavit ex eo insidias struere fratri clam palamque. Titus had displayed a spirit of brotherly affection (pietas) towards Domitian at the beginning of their father's reign by interceding for him when unfavourable rumours had reached Vespasian about him (Tac. H. iv 52). A remark which Pliny (Ep. iv 9, 2) makes about Julius Bassus, "Titum timuit ut Domitiani amicus," suggests that the forbearance of Titus towards his brother was not extended to his brother's friends.

p.note: : = palam, aperte, "openly and avowedly"; cf. Sen. Ερ. 14, Macrob. S. ii 9. Apuleius (Apol. 2) uses de professo. The passive sense of the deponent ptc. professus is first found in Ov. Am. iii 14, 6, solaque famosam culpa professa facit. See Neue-Wagener, Formenl. iii 43. Similar adverbial phrases used by Suet. are ex compacto, ex improviso, ex inopinato, ex composito, ex destinato.
: presumably to join some army in the provinces and lead it against Titus. 501.

: such "sequestration" was a thinly disguised form of relegatio (Vesp. 15, n.), as it really banished a person by sending him away from Rome under some specious pretext; cf. Oth. 3, 2, sepositus est per causam legationis in Lusitaniam: Aug. 65, 1, Agrippam Surrentum. Tacitus mentions several instances; e.g. A. iv 44, hunc seposuit Augustus in civitatem Massiliensem, ubi specie studiorum nomen exilii tegeretur. seposuit On

: the titles consors imperii (Oth. 8, 1) and particeps imperii (Tit. 6, 1, Dom. 2, 3) are used indifferently of the emperor's co-regent by Suet., Tac., and other authors. Under the constitution of the Principate the Princeps was given no right of appointing a successor, and Augustus had recourse to a consortium imperii, the co-regent being invested with extraordinary tribunician and pro-consular powers and placed in a position above all other magistrates, second only to the Princeps. Mommsen compares the relation of the co-regent to the Princeps with that of the praetor to the consul (Staatsr. ii³ 1146). the death of the Princeps, the co-regent, though having no legal claim, in practice succeeded to the vacant throne, unless prevented by revolution. See also Dom. 15, 1. In spite of the protestations of Titus mentioned here by Suetonius, he did not in reality associate Domitian in the government of the Empire. Neither the proconsulare imperium nor the tribunicia potestas was conferred upon him. He did not allow him to have the title of Imperator (allowed by Vespasian to Titus, see on c. 6, 1); this is shown by inscriptions in the reign of Titus, e.g. C.I.L. iii 318 (80 A.D.) where Domitian appears merely as "Caesar, Divi filius, Domitianus, consul VII, princeps iuventutis." ..

p.mentioned: ut mutuo erga se animo vellet esse
p.note: : for the constr. cf. Tac. H. iv 49, nec ambigitur militem alienato erga Vespasianum animo fuisse; for the use of mutuus cf. Cic. Fam. v 2, 1, Quod autem ita scribis, “pro mutuo inter nos animo,” quid tu existimes esse in amicitia “mutuum” nescio; equidem hoc arbitror, cum par voluntas accipitur et redditur: Catull. 45, 20, mutuis animis amant amantur: Hor. C. iv 1, 30, Iam nec spes animi credula mutui, "the fond hope of finding a heart to answer mine'' (Wickham): Cic. Att. xvi 16 a, tua voluntas erga me meaque erga te par atque mutua. Modderman, who asserts that mutuus animus erga aliquem is meaningless, would read mutato.

: "he was cut short (taken off) by death"; cf. Iul. 44, 4, talia agentem atque meditantem mors praevenit: Tib. 62, 3, nisi eum mors praevenisset: Justin 32, 3, peregissetque ultionem, nisi morte praeventus fuisset. Sallust once (Iug. 71) uses praevenio; it is not found in Cic. or Caes.

: Titus, like Agricola, was “felix opportunitate mortis” (Tac. Agr. 45). Ausonius, Caes. xi, addresses him as "Felix imperio, felix brevitate regendi”; cf. Dio lxvi 18, quoted on c. 1. For the modal abl. cf. Tib. 41, magno dedecore imperii nec minore discrimine: Claud. 16, 2, sed suo maiore dedecore. Bagge (De elocutione Suet., p. 82) says that in these passages the omission of cum is contrary to the usage of the best prose writers. But in class. Lat., when the modal abl. has an attribute with it, cum is more frequently omitted, and in Cic. we find cum sometimes used and sometimes omitted in the same expressions; e.g. Cat. ii 21, minore dolore perire: Cluent. 30, maximo cum dolore emori: Rep. 6, 15, celeritate mirabili: N.D. ii 97, cum admirabili celeritate. See Kühner-Stegmann, i 410.

: the spectacles which Titus gave at the opening of the new amphitheatre and baths in '80 A.D. (see c. 7, 3) lasted 100 days (Dio lxvi 25). It was not till the summer of 81 that he went to the Sabine territory and died there, so that Suetonius is inaccurate in his statement here. Titus was present at the meeting of the Collegium of the Fratres Arvales on May 19, 81 A.D. (C.I.L. vi 2060, Newton 1'60).
: see on Dom. 23, 1.

: Dio lxvi 26, διατελέσας δὲ ταῦτα, καὶ τῇ γε τελευταίᾳ ἡμέρᾳ καταδακρύσας, ὥστε πάντα τὸν δῆμον ἰδεῖν, οὐδὲν ἔτι μέγα ἔπραξεν, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐπιγιγνομένῳ ἔτει . . καθιερώσας ὅσα εἴρηται, μετήλλαξεν (excessit, obiit) ἐν τοῖς ὕδασιν ἐν οἷς καὶ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ. The ὕδατα mentioned by Dio as the scene of the deaths of Vespasian and Titus are the medicinal springs of Cutiliae near Reate; see Vesp. 24.

: his Sabine property at Reate (Vesp. 1, 2). For Sabini in the sense of a Sabine estate cf. Hor. C. ii 18, 14, satis beatus unicis Sabinis, the property in a district being described by the name of the people in the district (see Page on Hor. l.c.; Mayor on Plin. Ep. iii 4).
: = petiit, cf. Oth. 7, 1.

: for the indicative see on Vitell. 14, 4, exacerbatus, quod propositus est. The escape of a victim about to be sacrificed was always a dirum omen. The victim which broke away was called effugia, and the auspices at which the mischance occurred were called piacularia auspicia as requiring expiatory offerings; cf. Festus p. 245, Piacularia appellantur auspicia cum aut hostia ab ara fugit, aut percussa mugitum dedit, aut in aliam quam oportuit partem corporis cecidit. Escapes of victims from the altar are mentioned in Iul. 59; Galb. 18, 1; Тас. Н. iii 56; Liv. xxi 63; Verg. A. ii 223; Luc. vii 165; Sil. Ital. v 63, xvi 264. ..

: cf. Verg. G. i 487 (describing the portents of Caesar's death), non alias caelo ceciderunt plura sereno | fulgura. Often we find this regarded as a favourable sign; e.g. Ennius Ann. 155, сит tonuit laevum bene tempestate serena: Xen. Hell. vii 1, 31, ἐξ αἰθρίας ἀστραπάς τε καὶ βροντὰς λέγουσιν αἰσίους αὐτῷ φανῆναι : Hom. Od. xx 112 sqq.; Ov. F. iii 370. Horace (C. i 34) professes that he was converted from atheism by this phenomenon.

: cf. Claud. 39, 1, postero statim die "on the very next day'": Ner. 6, 2, primo statim conatu. Similarly statim is joined with the participle and not with the principal verb, in order to fix more closely the time-relation; e.g. Liv. xxviii 7, 9, quod viso statim hoste in deditionem concessissent: Suet. Aug. 28, 1, de reddenda re p. bis cogitavit: primum post oppressum statim Antonium, etc. Kühner-Stegmann, i 789.

: manere is often used in the sense of pernoctare, and in post-class. authors mansio (μονή) means "night-quarters" (statio nocturna, σταθμός); distance was measured by mansiones, stations, day's journeys, e.g. Plin. N.H. xii 52, a quo (monte) octo mansionibus distat regio.
: for this very rare use of nancisci cf. Nep. Att. 21, nactus est morbum: [Suet.] vit. Verg. 35, languorem nactus est.

: pallula, which in Plautus is used for a small cloak, here means a curtain, a sense which is attested for palla (Sen. Ira 3, 22, 2, сит inter dicentes et audientem palla interesset: Gloss. Philox. παραπέτασμα, velum, palla). Of the many variants in the MSS. (paludamentis, pellibus, palliolis, plagulis, etc.) plagulis is read in most of the old editions, plagula being used for the hanging or coverlet of a lectus (Liv. xxxix 6, 7; Non. 86, 7;378; 537, 20). The lectica was roofed with an arch (arcus) of leather (pellis) and there were horizontal curtain-rods from which the curtains (vela, pallulae, plagulae) fell; cf. Mart. xi 98, 11, lectica nec te tuta pella veloque | nec vindicavit sella saepius clausa. A newer variety of lectica had windows made of lapis specularis (talc?) which opened or shut (Juv. iv 21, cf. iii 242). See Daremberg-Saglio, iii 1005; Marquardt, Privatl.2 738. ..

: Dio lxvi 26, ὁ δ' οὖν Τίτος ἀποψύχων εἶπε μὲν ὅτι “Εν μόνον ἐπλημμέλησα. τί δὲ δὴ τοῦτο εἴη οὐ διεσάφησεν, ἀλλ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ἄλλος οὐδεὶς ἀκριβῶς ἀνέγνω· οἱ μὲν γὰρ τό, οἱ δὲ τὸ κατείκασαν. Dio says that the prevalent opinion was that Titus' one regret was having had intercourse with Domitian's wife, but he himself inclines to the view that the regret was for not having put Domitian to death for plotting against him, his forbearance exposing the Empire to such a successor. Ausonius (Caes. xi) refuses to believe Titus guilty of any offence: Unum dixisti moriens te crimen habere: | sed nulli de te, non tibi credidimus ("but we believe none speaking thus of thee not even thee thyself'"). Duruy (Hist. des Romains iv 674) suggests that the unum factum paenitendum was the putting to death of Caecina without trial (Tit. 6, 2); and other equally improbable conjectures have been hazarded. See Henderson, Five Roman Emperors p. 10.
: an example of the fondness of Suetonius for the perf. subj. instead of the normal pluperf. or imperf. See App. i. § 9. с.
: cf. Ner. 35, 5, persancte iurasset: Ter. Нес. 771, deierat persancte. Suetonius also uses perindigne, perraro, persaepe.
: see Dom. 3, 1.

: cf. Iul. 30, 1, bello vindicaturus, si quid gravius a senatu constitutum esset. This use of the fut. participle as apodosis to express the inference from a hypothetical proposition is first found in Livy (e.g. iii 60, egreditur castris Romanus, vallum invasurus, ni copia pugnae fieret) and occurs frequently in later writers (e.g. Tac. A. i 36, si omitteretur ripa, invasurus hostis). See Draeger, Hist. Synt. ii² 754.

: there are many conflicting accounts of the cause of Titus' death. Dio (lxvi 26) says that rumour (ἡ φήμη) attributed it to Domitian, who plunged him into a vessel full of snow while he was still breathing (cf. Cedren. p. 179), but that some writers stated that he died of disease. Suetonius (Dom. 2, 3) says that Domitian ordered the attendants of Titus to abandon him before he was dead. Aur. Vict. (Caes. 10, 11) declares that Domitian poisoned him, but in Epit. 10, 15 we are told that he died of fever. Plutarch (de Sanitate 3) cites Titus as an example of the fatal use of the bath in sickness, and mentions that this was the view of those who had tended him. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vi 32) says that Domitian poisoned him with a poisonous fish called λαγῶς θαλάσσιος (lepus marinus); so too Tzetzes (Chil. vi 278): Τίτος δὲ θνῄσκει βεβρωκὼς λαγῶν τῶν θαλασσίων. Suidas (s.v. Δομετιανός) repeats the poisoning charge; cf. Herodian iv 5, 6. The Jews believed that Titus' early death was a vengeance from Heaven for the sacking of Jerusalem; cf. the fantastic account in the Jewish Talmud which is thus given by Duruy: “Les Juifs en savaient bien plus long sur cette mort prématurée, et le Talmud raconte encore que Titus, retournant en Italie avec les vases sacrés ravis par lui dans le temple de Jéhovah, fut assailli par une furieuse tempête: 'Le Dieu des Juifs, s'écriat-il, n'a donc de force que sur la mer où il a déjà englouti Pharaon. S'il est vraiment Dieu, qu'il me combatte sur terre.' A ces mots une voix répondit: 'Méchant, fils de méchant, J'ai donné la vie à une créature infiniment petite, c'est elle qui combattra pour moi. ' Dès que Titus eut touché le rivage d'Italie, un moucheron entra dans ses narines et monta dans son cerveau qu'il rongea durant sept années. Un jour que le prince passait devant la boutique d'un forgeron, le bruit du marteau sur l'enclume arrêta l'insecte et l'atroce souffrance. Titus alors donna quatre pièces d'argent par jour à un homme qui se tint près de lui en frappant incessamment sur une enclume. Pendant un mois, le moyen réussit; mais au bout de ce temps l'insecte, accoutumé au bruit, se rémit à ronger. Quand Titus mourut, on ouvrit son crâne et on y trouva un moucheron gros comme une hirondelle, armé d'ongles de fer et d'un bec d'airain” (Hist. des Romains, iv 676 sq.).

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 15, in eodem, quo pater, apud Sabinos agro febri interiit: Oros. vii 9, 14, in eadem villa, qua pater eius, morbo absumptus est: Euseb.-Hieron. ad a. 2096 (81 A.D.), Titus morbo periit in ea villa, qua pater eius, anno aetatis xlii: Eutrop. vii 22, morbo periit in ea, qua pater, villa. This villa was at Aquae Cutiliae, a pagus in the ager Reatinus (see Vesp. 24). The omission of the prep. with the rel. is regular where the same verb is either repeated or understood in the rel. clause; e.g. Cic. Tusc. i 94, in eadem brevitate, qua illae bestiolae, reperiemur: id. Legg. iii 33, in ista sum scientia, qua te fuisse semper scio. ... ..

: Titus died on Sept. 13, 81 A.D.; his reign began on June 24, 79 A.D., the day after Vespasian's death (Vesp. 24). Dio (lxvi 26) agrees with Suetonius that Titus reigned for 2 yrs. 2 m. 20 d. Eutropius (vii 22) inaccurately says 2 yrs. 8 m. 20 d.; Joh. Antioch. (Müller, Fr. Hist. Gr. iv 579) 2 yrs. 8 m.; Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 5, biennio post, ac menses fere novėm interiit, but [Aur. Vict.] Epit. xi, imperavit annos duos, et menses duos, diesque viginti. Ausonius (258, 11) is writing with poetic freedom when he says "Ter, dominante Tito, cingit nova laurea Ianum” (referring to the custom of the new consul putting a fresh wreath on the statue of Janus on January 1).

: Dio (l.c.), Euseb.-Hieron., and Eutrop, agree with Suetonius that Titus died in his 42nd year; but the statement does not tally with the date of the birth of Titus given by Suetonius (c. 1), viz. Dec. 30, 41 A.D., for if that date were correct, he would only have been in his 40th year as Aur. Vict. says, Caes. 10, 5, anno aevi quadragesimo interiit (but Epit. 10, 1, vixit annos quadraginta unum). That he was born in 39, and not in 41, is shown by Dio (lxvi 18) who gives his age at his accession as 39 yrs. 5 m. 25 d. (see on c. 1). Similar inconsistencies on the part of Suetonius occur with regard to Galba (see on Galb. 23), Otho (Oth. 11), and Vitellius (Vitell. 18). Other examples of his chronological carelessness are: (a) in Ner. 7 he says that Nero was in his eleventh year when he was adopted by Claudius, whereas we know from Tac. A. xii 25 that the adoption took place in 50 A.D., while Nero was born on Dec. 15, 37 A.D. (Ner. 6); (b) in Claud. 27 he says that Britannicus was born on the 20th day of the reign of Claudius and in his second consulship, whereas Claudius began to reign on Jan. 25, 41 A.D. (Claud. 10), and his second consulship did not begin till 42 (Nipperdey and Smilda would delete inque secundo consulatu).

p.mentioned: non secus atque in domestico luctu maerentibus
p.note: : Eutrop. vii 22, tantus luctus eo mortuo publicus fuit, ut omnes tamquam in propria doluerint orbitate: Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 6, huius sane mors adeo provinciis luctui fuit, uti orbatum orbem deflerent: Epit. 10, 16, huius mors vix credi potest quantum luctus urbi provinciisque intulerit, adeo ut eum delicias publicas, sicut diximus, appellantes, quasi perpetuo custode orbatum terrarum orbem deflerent: Oros. vii 9, 14, cum ingenti omnium luctu morbo absumptus est. The sorrow of the people for the death of Titus has an earlier parallel in that for the death of Germanicus; cf. Tac. A. ii 82, where, after describing the indignation of the people at Tiberius' treatment of Germanicus, Tacitus says: Hos vulgi sermones audita mors (Germanici) adeo incendit ut ante edictum magistratuum, ante senatus consultum, sumpto iustitio desererentur fora, clauderentur domus. Passim silentia et gemitus, nihil compositum in ostentationem; et quamquam neque insignibus lugentium abstinerent, altius animis maerebant.

: the usual method of convening (vocare, convocare, cogere) the senate was by edict; cf. Iul. 80, 4, senatus Id. Mart. in Pompei curiam edictus est: Gell. N.A. iii 18, 7, (edicti) quo nunc quoque consules, cum senatores in curiam vocant, servandae consuetudinis causa tralaticio utuntur, verba haec sunt: "Senatores quibusque in senatu sententiam dicere licet”: Liv. xxiii 32, 3; xxviii 9, 5; Cic. Fam. xi 6, 2, cum tribuni pl. edixissent, senatus adesset a. d. xiii Kal. Ian. In cases of emergency the senators were summoned by criers (per praecones) sent round to their houses. See Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 918.

: the same account is given in Eutrop. vii 22, senatus, obitu ipsius circa vesperam nuntiato, nocte inrupit in curiam et tantas ei mortuo laudes gratiasque congessit, quantas nec vivo umquam egerat nec praesenti. Contrast the wild joy of the senate at the death of Domitian (Dom. 23, 1). Some MSS. (QSN) have the reading cucurrit, which appears in various early editions.
: because, as Eutropius (l.c.) tells us, it was nighttime. I adopt the punctuation advocated by Casaubon and Baumgarten-Crusius, connecting obseratis foribus with what precedes.

p.mentioned: tantas gratias egit laudesque congessit, quantas
p.note: : in the Editio Veneta of 1471 and other early editions we find gratias egit laudesque, quantas congessit, which is supported by Gronovius (on Liv. xxvi 48, dis immortalibus laudes gratesque egit) who cites Liv. vii 36, dis laudes gratesque agunt: xxvii 13, dis immortalibus, ut in tali re, laudes gratesque ago; Plaut. Trin. 821, Neptuno laetus lubens laudes ago et grates, gratiasque habeo. The MSS. of Suetonius are decisively against this reading.
